title: BxAgents
body: Get Started View on GitHub BxAgents is a conventions-based AI agent framework for BoxLang , built on ColdBox and BX AI . You describe an agent with files and folders - not a framework's API surface - and bxAgents build assembles a real, runnable ColdBox application out of it. Assembled at build time Discovery, validation and code generation run once , not on every boot. What you run afterwards is a plain ColdBox app. Folders are the API Agent.yaml and instructions.md are the only required files. Every other convention folder is optional and only shapes the output if it exists. Tools and skills Drop an @AITool -annotated function into tools/ , or a SKILL.md folder into skills/ - both are discovered and wired for you. Agents all the way down subagents/ nests the exact same convention tree, so a team of specialists is just more folders - built leaf-first. Twelve gateway types Telegram, Slack, Discord, Email, WhatsApp, Teams, Twilio, GitHub and Signal, plus http , cli and mock . A web chat UI, generated Ask for it in a gateways/ entry and the build produces a themeable, streaming chat front end with session history. Build one in four steps 1 Install BoxLang CommandBox install-bx-module bx-agents box install bx-agents 2 Scaffold bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 Then edit instructions.md and add whichever convention folders you need. 3 Build bxAgents build Discovery, validation, manifest, code generation - into .build/app/ . 4 Talk to it bxAgents chat # or serve it over HTTP: bxAgents serve --port=8080 Start from something, not nothing new doesn't only scaffold a blank agent - pick one of 8 built-in templates, clone an existing GitHub repo, or install a ForgeBox package instead. 8 built-in templates --template=webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent - real, working content layered on the same base skeleton. Clone a GitHub repo --repo=owner/repo - a bundled JGit client clones it; no git binary required. Install from ForgeBox --forgebox=<slug> - talks to ForgeBox's REST API directly; no box CLI required. See Agent Templates for every generated file in detail, and how to publish your own. A chat UI you didn't have to build Set exposes: "webui" on a gateway and the build emits a complete front end - conversation history, streaming replies, light/dark theming and a mobile layout - wired to your agent. It is generated CSS and generated markup - themeable from a gateways/ entry , with no front-end build step of your own. What build actually produces Your convention tree, and the plain ColdBox application build turns it into. your-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml # name, model, description ├── instructions.md # the system prompt ├── tools/ # @AITool functions ├── skills/ # SKILL.md capabilities ├── subagents/ # nested agent trees ├── gateways/ # HTTP/MCP/chat exposure ├── schedules/ # a real ColdBox scheduler ├── mcp/ # MCP servers you host ├── interceptors/ # lifecycle hooks └── modules/ # module dependencies .build/app/ ├── Application.bx ├── config/ │ ├── ColdBox.bx │ ├── WireBox.bx │ ├── Router.bx │ └── Scheduler.bx ├── agent/ │ └── GeneratedAgentFactory.bx ├── tools/ skills/ mcp/ ├── handlers/ interceptors/ └── index.bxm Why assemble at build time instead of at request time? Most agent frameworks wire tools, skills, routes and schedules together at request time , on every boot. BxAgents does the opposite: bxAgents build runs discovery, validation and code generation exactly once, producing a plain ColdBox application under .build/app/ . Starting it - via bxAgents serve , a real boxlang-miniserver process, or a portable .bxa deployed anywhere BoxLang runs - is then just booting an ordinary app. No convention scanning, no dynamic file walking, no build-time work deferred into the request path. Start with one file Only Agent.yaml is required. instructions.md is optional - set instructions directly in the YAML, or drop the file in and let the build wire it in. Every other folder only affects the generated output if it exists and has content in it - so you add conventions as you actually need them. YAML by default, a class when you need code Agent.yaml holds the agent's settings - most agents are a few lines of it. When the definition needs code (hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code), Agent.bx extends BX AI's own AiAgent directly - the build instantiates your class, so what you write is what runs. See Agent.yaml and Agent.bx . Reach it from anywhere Chat platforms Nine push-style gateways - Telegram, Slack, Discord, Email, WhatsApp Cloud, Teams, Twilio, GitHub and Signal - coordinated by one session with queue / steer / interrupt policies. HTTP and MCP Expose the agent over HTTP routes, or host local MCP servers from mcp/ so other clients can call your tools. Ship it Package a portable .bxa and deploy it with local , ssh , docker , digitalocean , ftp or sftp - secrets stay environment variables, never build artifacts. Check your setup at any time Where to go next Installation Install BoxLang, BX AI and BxAgents. Quick Start Scaffold, build and chat with your first agent. Conventions One page per convention folder, start to finish. The Build Pipeline Exactly what build does, in order. CLI Reference Every verb and its flags. Agent Templates Every built-in starter, GitHub/ForgeBox sourcing, and publishing your own. Deployment & Secrets Package a .bxa and ship it, safely. Every convention folder also has a working, buildable sample under examples/ .

title: Agent Templates
body: Agent Templates bxAgents new creates a project one of three mutually exclusive ways - see CLI Reference for the exact flag syntax and validation rules. This page goes deep on all three: exactly what each built-in --template generates, what a --repo / --forgebox source needs to look like to work as a project source, and how to build and publish one of your own. A template is the shape a project starts from. The new wizard lets you pick one (a single agent, a team, a scheduled agent, an MCP server) and then adds the tools, MCP servers, channels and deploy target you choose on top, so a template and those choices combine. The channel starters below ( slack-bot , telegram-bot , github-bot , webui-chat ) are the same thing as picking that channel in the wizard. bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 --template=<name> # a built-in starter bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # clone a GitHub repo bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug # install a ForgeBox package Every path lands on the same thing: a directory containing an agent definition (an Agent.yaml , or a class-based Agent.bx ) at its root, ready for bxAgents build . What differs is where that definition (and everything around it) comes from. The 8 built-in --template starters Every template starts from the exact same base skeleton - Agent.yaml , instructions.md , every empty convention folder , a ready-to-run tests/ folder, a .env (declaring BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime , with room for your API keys) and a .gitignore - then layers a small, specific amount of pre-wired content on top. Add --class to any --template to get the class-based Agent.bx form of the root definition (and of the subagents the multi-agent template scaffolds) instead of Agent.yaml ; everything else is unchanged. None of them need a validator change: each one's extra content reuses a config shape ProjectValidator already accepts, so a scaffolded project of any template validates cleanly by construction. phosphor-duotone:seedling minimal The bare skeleton. Nothing extra. webui-chat A browser chat UI at /chat. slack-bot A Slack Socket Mode channel adapter. telegram-bot A Telegram long-poll channel adapter. github-bot A GitHub issue/PR webhook adapter. mcp-server An example tool exposed as an MCP server. scheduled A real ColdBox Scheduler calling the agent. multi-agent Two subagents, wired via subAgents. minimal The default when --template is omitted entirely. This IS the base skeleton described above - no extra files. Use it when you're starting from a blank agent and adding conventions yourself as you need them. webui-chat Adds gateways/webui.bx , exposing the built-in web chat UI at /chat : // gateways/webui.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat" }; } } After bxAgents build && bxAgents serve , the agent is reachable at http://localhost:8080/chat - a real static chat page backed by a generated SQLite-based conversation store. No apiKeyEnvVar / users are configured out of the box, so the page is open by default; see The web chat UI for locking it down. slack-bot Adds gateways/slack.bx , a push-style Slack channel adapter (Socket Mode - a persistent websocket, no public webhook needed): // gateways/slack.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "slack", botTokenEnvVar : "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN", appTokenEnvVar : "SLACK_APP_TOKEN" }; } } Also appends matching stub lines to .env : # Slack gateway (gateways/slack.bx) - see https://api.slack.com/apps SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=xoxb-... SLACK_APP_TOKEN=xapp-... Fill in both real values from a Slack app with Socket Mode enabled before bxAgents serve - see Slack for the app-configuration steps. telegram-bot Adds gateways/telegram.bx , a push-style Telegram channel adapter (long-poll via getUpdates ): // gateways/telegram.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "telegram", botTokenEnvVar : "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" }; } } Also appends a matching stub line to .env : # Telegram gateway (gateways/telegram.bx) - from @BotFather TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=... Get a token from @BotFather and drop it in before serving. github-bot Adds gateways/github.bx , a push-style GitHub channel adapter (webhook-driven, @mention -gated issue/PR comment threads): // gateways/github.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "github", tokenEnvVar : "GITHUB_TOKEN", webhookSecretEnvVar : "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET", botNameEnvVar : "GITHUB_BOT_NAME" }; } } Also appends matching stub lines to .env : # GitHub gateway (gateways/github.bx) - a PAT with repo/issues+PR read+write scope GITHUB_TOKEN=... GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=... GITHUB_BOT_NAME=... GITHUB_TOKEN needs a PAT with repo + issues/PR read-write scope; GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET is whatever you set the repo's webhook signing secret to; GITHUB_BOT_NAME is the account name the bot replies as, used to gate on @mention . See GitHub for the webhook setup. mcp-server Adds an example MCP tool server plus a gateway entry exposing it: // mcp/exampleServer.bx class { function configure() { return { description : "Example MCP tool server", version : "1.0.0" }; } } // gateways/mcpExpose.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp", target : "exampleServer" }; } } target names the mcp/* entry to expose - here, the example server above. After build / serve , any MCP-speaking client can connect at /mcp . The example server registers no tools yet: write @AITool functions under tools/ and list their names in a tools: [ ... ] array in mcp/exampleServer.bx (or add more mcp/*.bx files), per mcp/ . scheduled Adds a real, hand-written ColdBox scheduler calling the agent on a timer: // schedules/Scheduler.bx class extends="coldbox.system.web.tasks.ColdBoxScheduler" { function configure() { task( "example" ) .call( () => getInstance( "my-agent" ).run( "Give me a status update" ) ) .everyDayAt( "00:00" ) } } ( getInstance(...) 's argument is always the scaffolded agent's own name , so it resolves the correct WireBox binding key.) This is real schedules/ content, not a placeholder - edit configure() directly to add/change tasks using ColdBox's own scheduler DSL ( everyMinute() , everyHourAt() , cron(...) , etc.). multi-agent The one template that changes the root Agent.yaml itself, rather than only adding files alongside it. It declares two subagents with a subAgents list: # Agent.yaml name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 subAgents: [ researcher, writer ] environments: # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider. test: model: mock/mock-model ...and scaffolds both as real, working subagent folders: subagents/ ├── researcher/ │ ├── Agent.yaml │ └── instructions.md └── writer/ ├── Agent.yaml └── instructions.md Each subagent's own Agent.yaml is a complete, buildable agent (always against the mock provider - a subagent here is a demonstration of the delegation shape, not a working agent out of the box): # subagents/researcher/Agent.yaml name: researcher description: "Gathers facts on a topic. Does not write final prose - that's the writer's job." model: mock/mock-model researcher gathers facts; writer turns findings into final prose - a minimal two-role delegation example. See subagents/ for how the subAgents list (folder names to wire) differs from super.init() 's own subAgents argument in a class-based Agent.bx (already-built AiAgent instances), and the multi-agent-team example for a fuller walkthrough. Sourcing a project from GitHub ( --repo ) bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # or a full URL: bxAgents new my-agent --repo=https://github.com/owner/repo-name.git Instead of scaffolding from a built-in template, --repo clones an existing repository and uses it as the new project directly. Cloning is done with a bundled JGit dependency ( org.eclipse.jgit:org.eclipse.jgit , from Maven Central) - no git binary needs to be installed or on PATH ; the git client ships inside the module's own jar. What makes a repo a valid template: an Agent.yaml (or Agent.bx ) at the repository's root, same as any scaffolded project. Beyond that, there's no special manifest or marker file to add - any BxAgents project (yours, a colleague's, an example from examples/ ) is already a valid --repo source as-is. What happens on clone, in order: owner/repo-name shorthand resolves to https://github.com/owner/repo-name.git ; a value already containing :// or starting with git@ is used as-is (so a self-hosted GitLab/Bitbucket/etc. HTTPS URL works too, not just GitHub). Refuses to run if the target directory already exists and is not empty - nothing is ever cloned over existing files. Clones shallow ( --depth=1 - only the current state, no history) via JGit's cloneRepository() . Always deletes the resulting .git folder afterward, unconditionally - no flag to keep it. This is deliberate: a template repo's own git history and origin remote have no legitimate reason to survive into a fresh project, and leaving them in place is a real foot-gun (your project's first git init /commit/push could otherwise interact with the template's upstream repo instead of your own). If you genuinely want the source repo's git history, clone it manually with git clone instead of using bxAgents new --repo . Verifies an Agent.yaml or Agent.bx exists at the cloned root - if not, the whole operation fails with a clear error naming what's missing, rather than leaving behind a half-usable, non-BxAgents directory. Warning Cloning is anonymous HTTPS only - no credentials are passed to JGit today, so a private repository will fail to clone. Use a public repo, or clone a private one manually and bxAgents new isn't the right tool for that case yet. --model , --name , and --description are not required or used with --repo - the cloned project already defines its own Agent.yaml or Agent.bx (and therefore its own name/model). Passing --name / --description anyway produces a warning in the output rather than an error, and is otherwise ignored. The scaffolded- tests/ 's automatic box install step (and --skipInstall ) also don't apply here - a cloned project's own tests/ folder, if it has one, is left exactly as cloned. Sourcing a project from ForgeBox ( --forgebox ) bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug Installs a ForgeBox package - CommandBox's package registry, which can host a full app/project template, not just a library - and uses it as the new project. This talks to ForgeBox's own public REST API ( https://www.forgebox.io/api/v1 ) directly, using BoxLang's native bx:http / http() support - no box CLI is required . What makes a ForgeBox entry a valid template: an Agent.yaml (or Agent.bx ) at the root of its published archive (or nested exactly one folder deep - see the unwrapping note below). ForgeBox has a dedicated bxagents entry type for exactly this ("BxAgents" in the ForgeBox UI) - browsing it is the fastest way to find a starting point - but bxAgents new --forgebox itself doesn't filter or care about an entry's declared type at all when installing; it only cares whether the downloaded archive, once extracted, contains an Agent.yaml or Agent.bx . What happens on install, in order: Refuses to run if the target directory already exists and is not empty . GET /entry/<slug> looks up the package. A slug that doesn't exist fails clearly and immediately - no download is attempted. Resolves the current release's download URL from the entry's own latestVersion.downloadURL (falling back to the newest entry in its versions array if that's somehow missing). Downloads the archive and extracts it with BoxLang's own built-in extract() BIF (zip support - no bespoke unzip code involved). Unwraps one level of nesting automatically , if present: many ForgeBox archives (matching a typical GitHub zip export) wrap their entire contents in one top-level folder. If extraction produces exactly one top-level entry and it's a directory, its contents are moved up so the target directory itself ends up as the project root. Verifies an Agent.yaml or Agent.bx exists at the (possibly unwrapped) root - if not, the whole operation fails, since a ForgeBox slug could just as easily be an unrelated library rather than a project template. Same as --repo : --model / --name / --description are not required (warned-and-ignored if passed anyway - the installed project defines its own), and the auto- box install / --skipInstall step doesn't apply. Publishing your own template A BxAgents template - whether you'll share it via GitHub, ForgeBox, or both - is just an ordinary BxAgents project (an Agent.yaml at its root, plus whatever conventions it uses) with the specifics filled in for someone else to copy and adapt, rather than left as placeholders for you personally. 1. Build the project Start from any of the 8 built-in starters above (or from scratch) and shape it into what you want people to start from: bxAgents new my-template --model=openai/gpt-5 --template=<closest starting point> A few things worth doing deliberately, since someone else will bxAgents new --repo=... / --forgebox=... this and expect it to just work: Keep Agent.yaml generic and buildable out of the box. Don't hardcode a real API key or point at a paid-only model by default - the test environment's mock/mock-model override (already scaffolded) means bxAgents test still works with zero setup even if the real model needs a key nobody but you has yet. Ship a real instructions.md describing the agent's actual purpose, not the generic "You are a helpful AI agent" placeholder new scaffolds by default. Document required env vars in .env as commented stub lines ( SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=xoxb-... , etc.) exactly like the slack-bot / telegram-bot / github-bot templates do above - it's the first thing someone reads after cloning. Verify it from cold , the same way a stranger would receive it: rm -rf .build dist , then bxAgents build && bxAgents test (and bxAgents doctor to catch anything env/dependency-related) from a completely fresh checkout. Never commit .build/ , dist/ , or a real .env - the scaffolded .gitignore already covers all three; keep it. 2a. Publish it to GitHub Nothing BxAgents-specific is needed - push the project to a public GitHub repository with Agent.yaml at the root (or push a subtree; --repo only unwraps ForgeBox's own single-nesting convention, not arbitrary repo layouts, so keep Agent.yaml at the actual repo root). Anyone can then run: bxAgents new my-agent --repo=your-org/your-template-repo A short "Getting Started" section in the repo's own README.md (what env vars to set, which model to point at) goes a long way, since --repo doesn't read or surface anything from the README itself - it's purely for the human cloning it. 2b. Publish it to ForgeBox ForgeBox packages are described by a box.json at the project root - the same file CommandBox's own package system uses everywhere else. At minimum: { "name": "My BxAgents Template", "slug": "my-bxagents-template", "version": "1.0.0", "type": "bxagents", "shortDescription": "A short description of what this agent template does", "private": false } slug is the unique name people install with ( --forgebox=my-bxagents-template ) - it's also what getEntry() looks up, so pick one you're happy to keep. type should be bxagents - ForgeBox's own dedicated entry type for BxAgents projects/templates (run box forgebox types to see it alongside every other type). bxAgents new --forgebox itself never inspects type when installing, but declaring it correctly is what gets your template listed under ForgeBox's own "BxAgents" category instead of a generic one, so people can actually find it by browsing. Add descriptive keywords too (e.g. "boxlang" , "ai-agent" ), since that's what full-text search uses. version should be bumped ( box bump --patch / --minor / --major , from inside the template's own folder) each time you publish a change - bxAgents new --forgebox always installs whatever latestVersion currently resolves to. Then, from inside the project: box forgebox register # once, if you don't already have a ForgeBox account box publish publish reads readme / instructions / changelog files from the folder by convention and publishes them as the entry's description/installation notes/changelog - worth having a real README.md for the same reason as the GitHub path above. Once published, anyone can run: bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=my-bxagents-template Info bxAgents new --forgebox already unwraps one level of nesting automatically (see above), so you don't need box.json 's createPackageDirectory: false setting for this specific path to work - that flag only matters for box install 's own separate install conventions, not this module's installer.

title: Agent.bx
body: Agent.bx Most agents use Agent.yaml instead The default way to define an agent is a plain Agent.yaml . Reach for Agent.bx when the definition itself needs code: hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code, an overridden method, or detectEnvironment() . A folder holds one or the other, never both. The sections on the model slug , environment overrides , merge semantics and the always-on agent route below apply to both. Agent.bx is the advanced way to define an agent. A BxAgents project needs an Agent.yaml or an Agent.bx . It extends bx-ai's own AiAgent , so it is the agent - the build instantiates it rather than rebuilding one from a config struct, so what you write is what runs. Inherit and add whatever you need: private helpers, overridden methods, tools registered in code. Because it's a real class rather than a struct-returning descriptor, an IDE can introspect it like any other BoxLang class - jump to definition, autocomplete on inherited methods, the works. class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "my-agent", description : "A helpful assistant", instructions: "You are a helpful assistant.", model : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } } bxAgents new --class scaffolds exactly this shape (without --class , new scaffolds an Agent.yaml ). instructions.md is optional - set instructions directly in super.init() , or drop the file beside Agent.bx and let the build wire it in for you (see the table below). What the build layers on top of the class The rule: an explicitly declared convention wins; otherwise the class is in charge. So an agent that sets everything in its own init() gets nothing imposed on it, while one that sets the bare minimum still picks up the conventions it didn't speak for. Everything below is optional - declare a configure() returning any of these keys to override what the class itself set, or the matching instructions.md / tools/ / subagents/ convention folder: You declare The build emits If you don't declare it instructions.md withInstructions( fileRead( ... ) ) the class's own instructions stand model in configure() setModel( aiModel( ... ) ) the class's own model stands name / description in configure() setName() / setDescription() the class's own stand memory in configure() setMemory( ... ) the class's own stands the tools/ folder withTools( ... ) with that folder's tools always - withTools() appends in bx-ai rather than replacing, so tools your class registered itself are kept and the agent's own tools/ are added tools / toolOptions in configure() withTools( ... ) with each item@module / *@module listed, built with the module's options no module tools; see Tools and Tool options subAgents on the class, or subagents/ on disk addSubAgent( ... ) per child appended the same way checkpointer in configure() withCheckpointer( ... ) injected anyway if the class set none - see below Info The checkpointer is the one thing the build fills in unasked. An agent reachable from a gateway with no checkpointer has silently broken human-in-the-loop, so a class that set none still gets the cache default. A class that sets its own is left alone. Warning Deliberately not implemented by comparing your instance against bx-ai's DEFAULT_AGENT_* values. "Did the author mean this, or is it just the default?" is unanswerable, and an author who genuinely wanted the default name would find it silently replaced. Presence of an external declaration is a fact; intent behind a default value is not. The class is copied into the generated app at agent/classes/ and instantiated there by its own absolute file path (never a relative lookup that would depend on a registered mapping), exactly as tools/ , skills/ and mcp/ are copied - so a packaged .bxa carries it, and chat / invoke / serve all instantiate it the same way whether or not a real ColdBox container is booted. configure() (optional) - overriding what the class set A configure() method is entirely optional. Declare it only to override specific fields from outside the class - useful for keeping deployment-specific values (a different model per environment, say) out of the class body itself: class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "with-mcp-servers-agent", model : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } function configure() { return { mcpServers : [ "https://example.com/mcp", { url : "https://other.com/mcp", name : "other" } ] }; } } Field Type Notes name string Also becomes this agent's config/WireBox.bx binding key at build time ( getInstance( name ) ) - see schedules/ - so it must be unique across the whole project (root + every subagent); build fails if two agents share a name. model string A provider/model slug or a bare provider name. A profile (see Models and profiles ) can stand in for it. See below. description string Optional. subAgents array of strings Names of sibling folders under the root project's subagents/ . See subagents/ . mcpServers array Remote MCP servers - each entry a URL string or { url, name } . See mcp/ . security struct Forwarded verbatim into the generated app's bxai module settings; bx-ai's own SecurityDirector turns it into guardrail middleware. Passthrough only - BxAgents has no own guardrails convention. memory string or struct The agent's conversation memory. A bare string is shorthand for the type ( "cache" ); a struct is { type, ...config } and is passed through to aiMemory() verbatim - e.g. { type: "cache", maxMessages: 50 } , or with summaryProvider / summaryModel / summaryThreshold to make the web UI's /compact functional. Applies per node, so a subagent can declare its own. checkpointer struct { type: "cache"\|"file"\|"jdbc", ...config } . Defaults to { type: "cache" } if omitted. Always applied - without one, human-in-the-loop approval flows through any gateway other than cli fail outright. gatewaySession struct { policy, maxQueueDepth } , both optional (default "queue" / 50 ). Only meaningful if the project has at least one push-style gateway entry - controls the generated GatewaySession 's policy for a second inbound message arriving on a thread that already has a turn in flight. policy must be one of reject / queue / steer / interrupt . agentApi struct { enabled, tokenEnvVar, tokens, profiles } , all optional. Controls the always-on agent route at /__bxagents . See The always-on agent route below. any other key any Merged and available in the resolved config struct, but not interpreted by BxAgents itself. The model slug model is BxAgents' own convention - bx-ai itself takes provider and model as two separate arguments to aiModel() . BxAgents splits the slug on the first / only , so a provider that itself contains a slash (like OpenRouter's openrouter/anthropic/claude-x ) still parses correctly: model value provider model openai/gpt-5 openai gpt-5 openrouter/anthropic/claude-x openrouter anthropic/claude-x mock/mock-model mock mock-model If model has no / at all, it must be a known core provider name (the provider's default model) - validation rejects anything else. The recognized core providers are: bedrock , cartesia , claude , cloudflare , cohere , deepseek , docker , elevenlabs , gemini , grok , groq , huggingface , minimax , mistral , mock , ollama , openai , openai-compatible , openrouter , perplexity , voyage (kept in sync with bx-ai's own CORE_PROVIDERS ). mock is a real provider, useful for tests and CI - it never makes a network call. This slug-splitting convention is what a configure() -declared model string goes through - super.init() 's own model argument instead takes a real AiModel instance directly ( aiModel( provider: "...", params: { model: "..." } ) ), since the class already speaks bx-ai's own API. Environment overrides Agent.bx may declare a method named after an environment (e.g. production() , development() , or any custom name) returning a struct of overrides - this works whether or not the class also declares a configure() : class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "override-agent", description : "An agent with an environment override", model : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } function production() { return { model : "openai/gpt-5-mini" }; } } The active environment is resolved with this precedence (highest wins): --environment CLI flag ( bxAgents build --environment=production ) Agent.bx 's own detectEnvironment() method, if it declares one BX_AGENTS_ENV environment variable "development" (default) detectEnvironment() For anything the first and third tiers can't express, Agent.bx may declare a detectEnvironment() method and decide for itself. Whatever it returns is taken as the environment name verbatim: class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "my-agent", model : aiModel( provider : "openai", params : { model : "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } function detectEnvironment() { return fileExists( expandPath( "/.production-marker" ) ) ? "production" : "development"; } } This mirrors ColdBox's own tier-1 convention (a config declaring detectEnvironment() has its return value taken verbatim), with two deliberate differences, both because this runs at build time: An explicit --environment flag outranks detectEnvironment() here, where ColdBox puts its own detect method first. A flag someone typed is the most specific statement of intent available. ColdBox's other detection tier - an environments struct of regexes matched against CGI.HTTP_HOST - is not supported. It cannot work here: the build runs in a CLI process with no HTTP host, so it would only ever describe the machine doing the building (a CI runner would resolve development for a production build). Returning a blank string, or anything that isn't a string, means "no opinion" and falls through to the next tier - so a project computing its environment from something absent on this machine degrades to the default rather than failing the build. A detectEnvironment() that throws is a different matter: that's a real bug in the project's own code, and build fails and says so. This is a build-time decision only, distinct from ColdBox's own runtime environment detection (the generated app reads getSetting("environment") on its own, per ColdBox's environments convention) - this precedence only decides which environment() override method on Agent.bx , and which boxlang-{env}.json / miniserver-{env}.json files, the build pipeline applies. If no method matching the active environment exists, no override is applied. Merge semantics The full resolution order (lowest to highest precedence) is: configure() (optional) the matching environment-override method, if any boxlang.json boxlang-{environment}.json miniserver.json miniserver-{environment}.json Struct keys are merged recursively - a nested struct in a higher-precedence source only overrides the keys it actually sets, leaving sibling keys from a lower-precedence source intact. Arrays and all scalar values are replaced whole , never appended or concatenated. boxlang.json / boxlang-{env}.json / miniserver.json / miniserver-{env}.json are all optional project-root JSON files, useful for config that's easier to express as data than as BoxLang code (e.g. model defaults): // boxlang.json { "modelDefaults": { "temperature": 0.7, "maxTokens": 1000 } } // boxlang-production.json { "modelDefaults": { "temperature": 0.2 } } Building with --environment=production here yields modelDefaults: { temperature: 0.2, maxTokens: 1000 } - the recursive merge kept maxTokens from the base file since boxlang-production.json never mentioned it. Warning Secrets (API keys, tokens) are never read or merged by BxAgents at build time - they stay external (an OS environment variable, .env , a platform secret manager) and are resolved live by bx-ai itself at runtime. See Deployment & Secrets . The always-on agent route Every built project exposes its root agent over HTTP at a fixed reserved path, whether or not it declares any gateways/ entries: POST /__bxagents/invoke POST /__bxagents/stream # SSE POST /__bxagents/batch GET /__bxagents/info These are the four sub-routes ColdBox's own toAi() terminator registers. The route exists so this module's own tooling always has an address to talk to - it's the service entrance, not your project's public API. A project's own public surface belongs in gateways/ , at whatever paths you choose. Run control Beside those four, a generated handler ( handlers/AgentApi.bx ) serves what a chat client needs to control a run. It is what chat --server and chat --connect use: POST /__bxagents/events # SSE: like /stream, plus tool and suspended frames POST /__bxagents/cancel # { threadId, reason? } POST /__bxagents/steer # { threadId, input } GET /__bxagents/pending # ?threadId= POST /__bxagents/resume # { threadId, decision } -> SSE, like /events GET /__bxagents/tools GET /__bxagents/profiles # the profiles a client may ask for GET /__bxagents/agent # name, model, what it can do GET /__bxagents/sessions # the caller's recent conversations GET /__bxagents/history # ?conversationId= what was said in one POST /__bxagents/clear # { conversationId } forget its messages POST /__bxagents/compact # { conversationId } summarize the older messages GET /__bxagents/notes # the caller's notes and the agent's, with how full they are POST /__bxagents/notes # { scope : "user" | "agent", text } POST /__bxagents/notes/update # { scope, id, text } POST /__bxagents/notes/remove # { scope, id } /events sends the frames of /stream ( thread first, chunk for each piece of the answer, done last) and adds: Frame Data tool { id, name, arguments, status, ms } , once with status: "running" and once with "ok" and the time it took suspended { threadId, pendingActions : [ { toolName, toolArgs } ] } when the run waits for a human decision error { message } cancel stops the run at its next checkpoint (before the next model call or tool call, not in the middle of a token). steer splices a message into a run in flight. resume takes approve , approve_session or reject and streams the rest of the turn. A run belongs to whoever started it: pending answers "nothing pending" and resume answers 403 to anyone else. Send a conversationId with /events to keep the turn in a conversation: the server lists it under the caller (the name of the token used, or api on an open route) and the agent's memory keeps its messages under the same id. sessions , history , clear and compact work on the caller's own conversations only; someone else's id is a 404 , the same as one that does not exist. They answer 404 when the server has no shared chat database, and compact reports available: false when the agent's memory has no summary model. The notes routes answer 404 for an agent that has no notes block. Each caller reads and changes their own user notes (the owner is the name of the token they used, or api on an open route) and the agent's notes. Any caller can add to either scope or edit a note; removing a note of the agent needs an admin token (a 403 otherwise), because it changes what every user's agent knows. These routes sit behind the same x-bxagents-token gate as the other four (a missing or wrong token is a 401 ), and agentApi.enabled: false removes all of them. Because the path is reserved, build rejects any gateways/ entry whose path is /__bxagents or sits underneath it. Two routes on one mount is a genuine conflict: one would silently shadow the other, and yours would be the one that never answers. agentApi configure() may return an agentApi struct to control it: Key Type Notes enabled boolean Default true . Set false to omit the route entirely - for a build going somewhere it has no business existing. tokenEnvVar string The name of an environment variable holding a shared secret. When set, every sub-route requires a matching x-bxagents-token request header. tokens boolean Default false . true also accepts the access tokens made with bxAgents token create . profiles list Default none. The profiles a client may ask for with options.profile on /events , and what GET /__bxagents/profiles lists (never a key). Any other profile is a 400 , so a caller cannot pick a model you did not offer. chat --connect uses this list for /profile . Each name must be declared in Agent.yaml , or default . function configure() { return { name : "my-agent", model : "openai/gpt-5", agentApi : { tokenEnvVar : "BXAGENTS_API_TOKEN" } }; } Because this comes from configure() , it scopes per environment with an environment override like any other key - so a project can leave the route open locally and require a token in production: function production() { return { agentApi : { tokenEnvVar : "BXAGENTS_API_TOKEN" } }; } The gate fails closed : if the named variable is unset or blank at runtime, nothing matches - it never degenerates into comparing "" to "" and letting every caller through. A request without a valid token gets a 401 with a small JSON body, and never reaches the agent. Warning tokenEnvVar names a variable , never the secret itself. build rejects a value that isn't a valid environment-variable name, precisely so a literal token can't be committed here by mistake. Only the variable's name is ever written into generated source. Access tokens for a deployed agent One shared secret ( tokenEnvVar ) is enough for a single caller. To let several people or machines in, each with a name you can revoke, turn on issued tokens: # Agent.yaml agentApi: tokens: true Make them where the agent's database is: on the server, or in the project before you pack it. bxAgents token create --name=laptop --expires=90d bxAgents token create --name=ci --scope=admin bxAgents token list bxAgents token revoke --name=laptop A token is shown once , when it is made. Only its SHA-256 is stored, so a stolen database file cannot be used to call the agent. The caller sends it in the x-bxagents-token header, or bxAgents chat --connect=<url> --token=<token> (or BXAGENTS_TOKEN ) does. The name is who is calling. A run belongs to the token that started it, and one token cannot answer another's pending approval. The scope is chat or admin . Revoking takes effect on the next request, without a restart. A token can also expire ( --expires=90d , 12h , 2w or a date). With tokens: true and no tokenEnvVar , a server with no tokens yet refuses everyone. With both, the shared secret works as an admin token, so a fresh deployment can be reached before the first token exists. The tokens live in the shared chat database ( data/chat.db ). On a deployed server run token with BXAGENTS_DB pointing at the file the app uses. Put HTTPS in front of any server a token travels to: a token on plain HTTP can be read on the wire. Info The route is bound to whatever host the miniserver is listening on - 127.0.0.1 by default, so nothing is reachable off the machine unless you deliberately expose it. tokenEnvVar is what matters once you do, and for any built .bxa artifact you deploy.

title: Agent.yaml
body: Agent.yaml Agent.yaml is the default way to define an agent. It is a plain YAML file - a name, a model, and any of the optional settings below - and the build turns it into a running agent. Most agents need nothing more than this file and an instructions.md beside it. name: support description: Answers customer questions about orders model: openai/gpt-5 environments: test: model: mock/mock-model bxAgents new scaffolds exactly this shape. When the definition needs real code (hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code), use the advanced option instead: a class-based Agent.bx , scaffolded with bxAgents new --class . Info A folder holds one agent definition. An Agent.yaml (or Agent.yml ) together with an Agent.bx in the same folder is an error - two definitions of one agent would leave it ambiguous which settings win - and build fails and names both files so you can keep one. This applies to the project root and to every subagent folder, and a project can mix the two: a YAML root with a class-based subagent, or the other way round. Settings Key Type Notes name string Also becomes this agent's config/WireBox.bx binding key at build time, so it must be unique across the whole project (root + every subagent). model string A provider/model slug, a bare provider name, or a model name when provider is set. See The model slug and Models and profiles . provider string The default provider, a bx-ai provider name. With model as a bare model name. See Models and profiles . params mapping Default request parameters, such as temperature . options mapping Default provider options, such as timeout . providers mapping Per provider params and options , by provider name. profiles mapping Named combinations of provider, model, params, options and apiKeyEnv . defaultProfile string The profile used when nothing asks for another. profile string The profile this agent uses. embeddings , speech , transcription , image mapping bx-ai's capability defaults: provider , model and a few settings each. description string Optional. instructions string Optional inline instructions. See Instructions . tools list of strings Module tools this agent gets, as item@module or *@module . See Tools . toolOptions mapping Options for a module's tools, keyed by module name. See Tool options . subAgents list of strings Names of sibling folders under the root project's subagents/ . See subagents/ . mcpServers list MCP servers - each entry a URL string, a mapping with url and the credentials the server wants ( token , headers , timeout ), or a mapping with command for a server that runs as a program ( env , cwd , prefix , toolFilter ). See mcp/ . security mapping Forwarded verbatim into the generated app's bxai module settings; bx-ai's own SecurityDirector turns it into guardrail middleware. memory string or mapping The agent's conversation memory. A bare string is the type ( cache ); a mapping is { type, ...config } and is passed through to aiMemory() . checkpointer mapping { type: cache\|file\|jdbc, ...config } . Defaults to { type: cache } if omitted. gatewaySession mapping { policy, maxQueueDepth } , both optional. See Agent.bx for the values; they are identical. agentApi mapping { enabled, tokenEnvVar, tokens, profiles } , all optional. See The always-on agent route . notes mapping Short notes the agent keeps about the user and its own work. notes: {} turns them on with the defaults. See Notes . environments mapping Per-environment overrides. See Environments . These are the same settings an Agent.bx 's configure() returns, so every behavior documented for them applies unchanged. Warning An unknown key is an error , and the message lists the valid ones. A typo such as modle: would otherwise do nothing, quietly. Settings that arrive in later releases (for example mcp ) are rejected the same way until they exist, rather than being silently ignored. Anything free-form belongs in an Agent.bx . A value of the wrong type (a text where a list belongs, say) and an empty value ( model: with nothing after it) are errors too. Tools An agent gets its own tools/ folder, and nothing else, unless it asks. The tools other modules provide (bx-ai's built-ins, bx-playwright , ...) are a catalog: they are available, but an agent only has the ones its tools: list names. Every entry is item@module , the key bx-ai keeps them under: name: support model: openai/gpt-5 tools: - now@bxai # one tool from one module - "*@bxplaywright" # every tool that module registered (quote it: * starts a YAML alias) Entry Gives the agent item@module that one tool *@module , or @module every tool the module registered Default. No tools: means only the agent's own tools/ . This holds for every subagent too: each one has its own tools/ and its own tools: . Naming a module validates it. If the module is not installed, or has no such tool, build and the generated app fail with a message that lists what the module does provide. A bare name is an error. now fails with a hint to write now@bxai . bx-ai would otherwise resolve it to whichever module registered a tool called now first. Own tools win. If a tool in the agent's tools/ has the same name as a module tool it selected, the own tool is used and the module tool is left out, with a warning in the bxagents-tools log. Each tool once. Listing a tool twice, or listing it along with a *@module that covers it, attaches it once. Tool options toolOptions configures the tools of a module, keyed by module name . Two modules take options: bxai , for its file tools , and bxplaywright , whose options are those of bx-playwright's playwright() : a profile (a name, or a list of names) and settings such as headless , baseURL , browser , viewport or device . tools: - "*@bxplaywright" toolOptions: bxplaywright: profile: mobile headless: false baseURL: ${env.APP_URL:http://localhost:8080} Each agent gets its own browser. The browser tools bx-playwright registers share one browser for the whole app. An agent that lists bxplaywright tools does not get those: it gets a fresh set built for it alone ( playwright( profile, options ).aiTools() ), so a root agent and its subagent never drive the same page. The browser opens when one of its tools is first used, not at startup. *@bxplaywright works with no toolOptions at all and uses the module's own settings. Environment values. ${env.NAME}` and `${env.NAME:default} are replaced with the environment variable when the app starts, never at build time, so a secret or a per-machine setting stays out of the project. A variable that is not set and has no default fails the agent at startup, naming it. Checked at build time. A key that is not a module the agent lists tools from, a module that takes no options, a key written as item@module , or an option bx-playwright does not have (the message lists the valid ones) is a build error. The module-wide settings (where browsers are installed, the default profile) stay in bx-playwright's own settings, not here. File tools bx-ai has 19 file tools ( readFile , writeFile , listDirectory , searchFiles , deleteFile , zipFiles and more), but it registers none of them. In BxAgents an agent gets them by listing them and naming the folders they may use in toolOptions.bxai.allowedPaths : tools: - readFile@bxai - listDirectory@bxai toolOptions: bxai: allowedPaths: - tmp # the system temp folder - cwd # the folder the agent is started from - /data/reports # or an absolute path Each agent gets its own tools, locked to its own folders. A path outside them is refused ( .. tricks included), and the tools are never put in the shared registry where another agent could pick them up. No folders, no tools. The tools exist only when allowedPaths is set, and an empty list is a build error, because bx-ai reads an empty list as "any path". Listing readFile@bxai with no allowedPaths fails with a message saying so. now@bxai , httpGet@bxai , webSearch@bxai and the rest of bx-ai's registered tools keep working as before, with or without toolOptions.bxai . *@bxai includes the file tools once allowedPaths is set. An entry may be ${env.NAME} to take a folder from the environment. bxAgents new can write all of this for you: see the new wizard . Notes An agent can keep short notes: things about the user ("prefers short answers") and things about its own work ("the repo uses Gradle"). They are off until the block is there: notes: {} notes: provider: sqlite # built in. Or a class implementing INotesProvider user: { limit: 1400 } # characters of user notes that go into the prompt agent: { limit: 2200 } # characters of agent notes tool: true # give the agent the remember and forget tools (default true) approveForget: true # a person approves what the agent forgets (default true) Key Default Notes provider sqlite sqlite keeps one row per note in the shared chat database . Any other value is the name of a class that implements INotesProvider and is created with ( config, agentName ) , for a notes service of your own. user.limit 1400 Characters of notes about the user. Each user has their own. agent.limit 2200 Characters of notes about the agent's work. Shared by everyone who talks to it. tool true remember (save or replace a note) and forget (remove one). Without them the notes are read-only for the agent and a person manages them. approveForget true A run that wants to forget stops for approval , like any tool that needs it. Saving a note needs none. How it works: Both scopes go into the system prompt as short lists, oldest first, within their limits. They are read once per conversation, so the prompt stays the same turn to turn (a provider's prompt cache keeps working) and a note saved now shows from the next conversation. A note is one line of at most 500 characters. Nothing is dropped silently: a note that does not fit the limit is refused, and the agent is told how full the notes are so it can replace or forget an older one. Who a user is : in bxAgents chat it is the operating system user ( --user=NAME changes it); on a server it is the name of the access token the caller used, or api when the route is open. The agent scope belongs to the agent's name . The terminal chat, the web chat and the server share one file, data/chat.db (see the SQLite store ). Manage them yourself with /remember and /notes in chat , with bxAgents notes from a shell, or over HTTP through the run-control routes . Instructions The agent's instructions are its system prompt. Put them in an instructions.md beside Agent.yaml , the usual choice because the file is plain Markdown and easy to edit: my-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml └── instructions.md For a short prompt you can write them inline instead: name: greeter model: openai/gpt-5 instructions: | You greet people by name. Keep it to one sentence. If both exist, instructions.md wins - the file is the more deliberate choice, so a stray instructions: line cannot override it. If neither exists, build fails and says so. Environments environments holds overrides keyed by environment name. It is the YAML spelling of the environment-override methods ( production() ) an Agent.bx can declare: name: support model: openai/gpt-5 environments: production: model: openai/gpt-5-mini staging: description: Staging copy The active environment is chosen with this precedence, highest first: the --environment CLI flag ( bxAgents build --environment=production ) the BX_AGENTS_ENV environment variable development Only the block for the active environment is applied, on top of the top-level settings; keys it does not mention are left alone. Each block accepts the same keys as the top level, except environments itself. bxAgents test builds against the test environment, which is why a scaffolded project carries a test block pointing at the mock provider: its tests need no API key or network access. Note An Agent.yaml cannot compute its environment. The detectEnvironment() method described under Environment overrides needs code, so a project that needs it uses an Agent.bx . The overrides then merge with boxlang.json , boxlang-{environment}.json , miniserver.json and miniserver-{environment}.json exactly as described in Merge semantics . Requirements Reading YAML needs the bx-yaml module, 1.1.0 or later . BxAgents bundles it, so there is nothing to install. Global YAML tags (such as !!java.io.File ) are rejected, so a cloned project's Agent.yaml cannot make the build instantiate arbitrary Java classes. YAML or Agent.bx? Use When Agent.yaml The agent is configuration: a name, a model, instructions, memory, subagents. This is almost every agent. Agent.bx The definition itself needs code: hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code, an overridden method, or detectEnvironment() . You can start with YAML and switch later: create the Agent.bx , move the settings across, and delete the Agent.yaml .

title: box.json
body: box.json BxAgents already bundles BX AI, ColdBox and the other modules agents use, so most agents need nothing more. When an agent needs a package that is not bundled, for example bx-playwright for browser tools, list it in a box.json at the project root and install it yourself: { "name": "support-bot", "dependencies": { "bx-playwright": "*" }, "devDependencies": { "testbox": "*" } } BxAgents never installs anything. Install packages the way you normally do, with CommandBox ( box install ) or the BoxLang binary ( install-bx-module bx-playwright --local ), from the project root. bxAgents new scaffolds a box.json for you, with TestBox as a development dependency installed into lib/testbox , and a .gitignore that already ignores lib/ and boxlang_modules/ . Commit box.json ; keep the installed folders out of version control. Where installed packages go What Folder in the project What build does with it BoxLang modules ( bx-playwright , ...) boxlang_modules/ BoxLang loads this folder from the project root, so chat , invoke and test find them. build copies it to .build/app/boxlang_modules , so serve and a packaged .bxa carry it too. ColdBox libraries and modules lib/coldbox , lib/modules/<name> Copied into the app over the bundled ones, so a project can add or override a library. Test tools (TestBox, ...) lib/<name> or tests/ Not copied: the app does not need them. Development dependencies A BoxLang module that is only in devDependencies is left out of .build/app , and the build says which. A module is matched to box.json by the slug in its own box.json , or by its folder name ( bxplaywright for bx-playwright ). One listed in both sections is kept. Using an installed module A module that registers tools, such as bx-playwright , is used by naming its tools in the agent's tools . If the module is not installed, the error says how to install it: tools: - "*@bxplaywright" Note box.json is different from modules/ , which holds ColdBox modules that are part of your project's own source.

title: CLI Reference
body: CLI Reference Usage: boxlang module:bxAgents <verb> [options] (or the shorter bxAgents <verb> [options] form - see Installation .) Global flags These are handled before verb dispatch and never reach a verb. Flag Effect -h , --help , help Print usage (every verb + description) and exit 0. Accepted in any position, so bxAgents clean --help prints usage rather than running clean . Also printed (exit 1) if no verb is given at all. -v , --version Print bxAgents v{version} and exit 0. Only meaningful as the very first token, so it never collides with package --version=1.0.0 . The banner At an interactive terminal, bxAgents --help and the end of the new wizard greet you with the BxAgents name in block letters, painted in a gradient picked at random from eight themes (Ocean, Fire, Sunset, Purple, Mint, Gray, Forest, Gold), the same idea as the ColdBox CLI's banner. It is never written to a pipe or a file. Setting Effect NO_COLOR , --no-color Same shape, no color TERM=dumb , output that is not UTF-8, or a terminal narrower than the art (76 columns) One plain line instead --no-banner , or BXAGENTS_BANNER=off No banner BXAGENTS_BANNER_THEME=Ocean Pin a theme instead of a random one, for a recording that comes out the same every time Every verb accepts --projectRoot=<path> (or a bare positional path as the first non-flag argument) to target a project other than the current directory. Precedence: --projectRoot flag > first positional argument > current working directory. Argument syntax Follows BoxLang's own documented CLI conventions: Form Result --option true --option=value / --option="quoted value" value (surrounding quotes stripped) -o=value short form with a value -o short form, true -abc combined shorthand: a , b , c all true --!option / --no-option negation, false anything else a positional (the first becomes the project-root fallback) Repeated options: last one wins. Note the first row: a bare --option is a boolean , not a way to pass the next token as its value. A flag that requires a value ( --model , --message , --password , --environment , --port , ...) is therefore rejected with an error when written bare, rather than silently becoming true : $ bxAgents new my-agent --model openai/gpt-5 Error: --model requires a value - write it as `--model=<value>`. Always use the --flag=value form. The space-separated form is not supported. Tab completion completions/ holds ready-made completion scripts for bash, fish and PowerShell. See Installation for the one-line setup of each. Verbs new Scaffold a new agent project. add Add a tool, interceptor, schedule, MCP server, gateway, subagent or skill to an existing project. skills Find, install, update and remove skills from skills.boxlang.io. build Run the full build pipeline. test Run your project's own tests/specs via TestBox. serve Launch a real boxlang-miniserver process. chat Interactive REPL against the built agent. invoke One non-interactive turn - for scripting/CI. package Package a built project into a .bxa. deploy Ship to a real deployment target. hash-password Hash a plaintext password for a webui users entry. token Issue, list and revoke access tokens for a deployed agent. notes Read and manage the notes an agent keeps. inspect Report how the agent is composed, from its source. clean Remove a project's .build/ and dist/ output. doctor Diagnose the runtime and project before build/serve surprise you. new Create a new agent project one of three mutually exclusive ways: scaffold it (answering questions at a terminal, or with flags), clone a GitHub repo, or install a ForgeBox package. # At a terminal: answer questions (see the new wizard guide) bxAgents new my-agent # Scaffold from flags (default template: minimal) bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 [--template=minimal|webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent] [--name=...] [--description=...] [--class] [--skipInstall] # The same, adding what the wizard would have offered bxAgents new my-agent --model=claude --with=time,search --search=brave --mcp=github --channels=web,telegram --guard=flag # Clone an existing GitHub repo bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # Install a ForgeBox package bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug With no --model , no --repo and no --forgebox , at a terminal, new runs the wizard . --no-wizard or --yes turns it off, --wizard turns it on even with a --model , and --no-tui asks the same questions as numbered lines. A --model on its own never starts it, since scripts have always had to pass one. The wizard's flags ( --with , --search , --files , --files-dir , --temperature , --max-tokens , --timeout , --memory , --mcp , --channels , --web-auth , --guard , --deploy and the deploy details) are listed in the wizard guide ; a bad value names the flag and what it accepts. They need Agent.yaml , so they cannot be combined with --class . --template , --repo , and --forgebox name three different project SOURCES - exactly one applies. Combining any two of them is an error. --template mode (the default when no source flag is passed at all - minimal ): --model is required when no questions are asked - a provider/model slug (see the model slug ). --name defaults to the target directory's own basename. Refuses to run if the target already contains an Agent.yaml or an Agent.bx . Creates Agent.yaml , instructions.md , every convention folder (empty), a root box.json ( testbox as a development dependency, installed into lib/testbox ), a ready-to-run tests/ folder ( tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx ), a .env declaring BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime (matching serve 's own scoped runtime home), a .gitignore ( .env , .build/ , dist/ , lib/ , boxlang_modules/ , editor files), and the standard dotfiles .editorconfig , .gitattributes , .bxlint.json , .markdownlint.json and a .boxlang.json listing every bx-ai setting at its default (the BoxLang runtime reads it when run from the project root; edit the values there). Never overwrites a file that already exists. BoxLang and boxlang-miniserver load a .env from the project root themselves, so the file also works for your API keys; BxAgents never reads, copies or packages it. --class (a bare boolean flag, like the others described above) writes the class-based Agent.bx instead of the default Agent.yaml , for agents whose definition needs code (hooks, dynamic instructions). It applies to the root and to any subagents a template scaffolds, and only to --template mode - not to --repo / --forgebox . --template picks one of 8 built-in starters, each layering a bit of pre-wired content on top of the base skeleton above (see Agent Templates for every generated file in full, plus how --repo / --forgebox sources work and how to publish your own): minimal - the bare skeleton, nothing extra. webui-chat - adds a gateways/webui.bx exposing the web chat UI at /chat . slack-bot - adds a gateways/slack.bx channel adapter, plus matching SLACK_BOT_TOKEN / SLACK_APP_TOKEN stub lines in .env . telegram-bot - adds a gateways/telegram.bx channel adapter, plus a matching TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN stub line in .env . github-bot - adds a gateways/github.bx channel adapter, plus matching GITHUB_TOKEN / GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET / GITHUB_BOT_NAME stub lines in .env . mcp-server - adds an example mcp/exampleServer.bx tool server and a gateways/mcpExpose.bx entry exposing it as an MCP server at /mcp . scheduled - adds a real schedules/Scheduler.bx calling the agent on a daily timer. multi-agent - adds a subAgents list to the root Agent.yaml declaring two subagents ( researcher , writer ), each scaffolded as its own real subagents/<name>/Agent.yaml + instructions.md . Also runs box install in the new project root, so bxAgents test works immediately with no separate install step. This is best-effort: if box isn't on PATH or the install fails, new still succeeds - the message just tells you to run it yourself. Pass --skipInstall to opt out of this step entirely. --repo mode ( --repo=owner/repo-name or a full URL): clones the repo via a bundled JGit dependency - no git binary needs to be installed. Always clones shallow (depth 1) and always strips the resulting .git folder afterward, so the new project starts with a clean history rather than staying tied to the template repo's own remote. Refuses to run into a directory that already exists and is non-empty, and fails clearly if no Agent.yaml or Agent.bx is found in the cloned repo. --forgebox mode ( --forgebox=<slug> ): installs a ForgeBox package by talking to ForgeBox's own REST API directly (no box CLI required). Fails clearly if the slug doesn't exist, the download fails, or the installed package has no Agent.yaml or Agent.bx at its root (unwrapping one level of nesting first, since many ForgeBox archives wrap their contents in a single top-level folder). Only --template mode needs --model ; --repo / --forgebox never require it, since the source project already defines its own. --name / --description are ignored (with a warning in the output) when --repo / --forgebox is used - the cloned/installed project defines its own. The box install convenience step (and --skipInstall ) only ever apply to --template mode - a cloned/installed project's own box.json (if it has one at all) is left untouched. add Add one thing to a project that already exists, asking the same questions new asks. Today that is a tool , an interceptor , a schedule , an mcp server, a gateway , a subagent , a skill , a profile , a provider or a capability . bxAgents add # pick what to add bxAgents add tool # asks for the name, function, description and arguments bxAgents add tool WeatherTools --function=getWeather --description="Get the weather for a city" --args="city, days:numeric" bxAgents add tool Pinger --agent=researcher # into subagents/researcher/tools/ bxAgents add tool Pinger --dry-run # show the file, write nothing The positional arguments are the kind and the name, so the project is found by --projectRoot=<path> or the current folder only. At a terminal, whatever is not given as a flag is asked, in the full-screen UI (or numbered lines with --no-tui ). With --yes , in a pipe or in CI nothing is asked: flags and defaults are used, and a required answer that is missing names the flag to pass. Questions end on a review of the files that will be written. Cancelling, with Esc or Ctrl+C, changes nothing. Nothing is overwritten. If a file already exists none are written and the error names it; --force replaces it. --dry-run prints each file with its text and writes nothing. add tool Creates tools/<Name>.bx with one @AITool function in the shape bx-ai documents : a docblock describing each argument, the annotation carrying the description the model reads, and typed required arguments from which bx-ai builds the tool's schema. Flag Meaning --name=<Name> The file name, or the second positional. Letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. --agent=<subagent> Whose tool it is. Asked only when the project has subagents; . (the default) is the root agent. --function=<name> The function the model calls. Defaults to the file name with a lower-case first letter. --description=<text> What the tool does. The model reads it to decide when to call the tool. Without it, and with nothing to ask, the file gets a TODO description and the output reminds you to replace it. --args=<list> Comma separated, each name or name:type ( string by default; numeric , boolean , array , struct , date and any also work). A tool belongs to the agent whose folder it is in and is attached to that agent automatically. Two tool files of one agent may not share a name, even in different subfolders, so a clash is refused here instead of at the next build . Check the result with bxAgents inspect --section=tools . add interceptor Creates interceptors/<Name>.bx with one method for each interception point you pick, and the @scope that the build splits on . bxAgents add interceptor AuditLogger --points=preProcess,onException --description="Log every request" bxAgents add interceptor AiWatch --scope=runtime --points=beforeAIModelInvoke,onAIError Flag Meaning --name=<Name> The file name, or the second positional. A name another interceptor already uses is refused. --scope=agent\|runtime agent (the default) is a ColdBox interceptor registered with the generated app when it starts; its methods take ( event, interceptData, rc, prc ) . runtime listens to the events bx-ai announces in the BoxLang runtime and takes the event data as its one argument; BxAgents copies it to .build/runtime-interceptors but does not register it for you. --points=<list> Comma separated interception points. The picker offers the common ones; any ColdBox core point ( agent ) or bx-ai event ( runtime ) can be named here, and a name that is not a point for that scope is refused. Defaults to preProcess ( agent ) or beforeAIModelInvoke ( runtime ). --description=<text> One line for the class's docblock. Optional. add schedule Adds a task to schedules/Scheduler.bx that sends the agent a message on a schedule. Only two things are asked: when it runs and what it says to the agent. Overlapping runs are always prevented ( .withNoOverlaps() ). bxAgents add schedule --when="weekdays 08:30" --prompt="Summarize yesterday's findings" bxAgents add schedule digest --when="every 15 minutes" --prompt="Check for new tickets" --agent=researcher bxAgents add schedule # asks how often, the details, a name, and what to say Flag Meaning --when=<phrase> When it runs, in one of the phrases below. At a terminal, leave it out and you are asked how often, then the details. --prompt=<text> The message sent to the agent each time. --name=<name> The task's name, or the second positional. Defaults to a name made from the phrase. A name already in the scheduler is refused. --agent=<subagent> Which agent runs it. Asked only when the project has subagents; . (the default) is the root agent. The task looks the agent up by its declared name , so renaming the agent means editing the task. Phrase Runs every 15 minutes , every 2 hours , every 1 days At that interval hourly , hourly :15 Every hour, on the hour or at that minute daily 09:00 Every day at that time weekdays 08:30 , weekends 10:00 Monday to Friday, or Saturday and Sunday weekly mon 09:00 Once a week ( mon tue wed thu fri sat sun ) monthly 1 09:00 Once a month on that day, 1 to 28 so that no month skips it first-business-day 09:00 , last-business-day 17:00 On that business day of each month Times are 24 hour HH:mm in the scheduler's timezone. There is no cron phrase: ColdBox's ScheduledTask has no cron method, so for anything else write the task by hand with its full DSL. If schedules/Scheduler.bx does not exist it is created. If it does, the task is added at the end of configure() and the rest of the file is left as it was. If configure() cannot be found, nothing is changed and the error carries the task to paste in. Scheduled tasks run while the app is served ( bxAgents serve ). Check the result with bxAgents inspect --section=schedule . add mcp Adds an MCP server in either direction: one the agent calls (written into Agent.yaml ), or one the project hosts ( mcp/<name>.bx ). bxAgents add mcp client github # a server from the catalog the new wizard uses bxAgents add mcp client --url=https://mcp.acme.dev/mcp --name=acme --auth=bearer --env=ACME_TOKEN bxAgents add mcp server tools --description="My tools" bxAgents add mcp # asks which way add mcp client adds an entry to the agent's mcpServers: list. A name from the catalog ( github , stripe , notion , atlassian , cloudflare , supabase , git ) fills in the address and the sign-in, or for a server that runs as a program on this machine ( git ) the command to start it and what it needs on the PATH; otherwise give --url . Flag Meaning --url=<address> A server not in the catalog. An address with a user name, password or key in it is refused: the secret belongs in an environment variable. --name=<label> A label for Agent.yaml ; it is not sent to the server. --auth=none\|bearer\|header\|basic How it signs you in. bearer writes token , header writes headers (name it with --header= ), basic writes user (with --user= ) and password . --env=<NAME> The environment variable that holds the key or password. Only the name goes in Agent.yaml , as ${env.NAME} ; an empty NAME= is added to .env for you to fill in. --timeout=<ms> Optional. --agent=<subagent> Which agent uses it; . (the default) is the root agent. add mcp server writes mcp/<name>.bx offering the project's tools through bx-ai's MCP server, and, unless you decline, a gateways/<name>Mcp.bx entry that serves it over HTTP. Flag Meaning --name=<name> The file name and the server's name. Defaults to tools . --description=<text> , --version=<x.y.z> What other agents see. --tools=<list> Which tools to offer. Defaults to all of the root agent's tools; a name that is not one of them is refused. --cors=<origin> Web origins allowed to call it from a browser; * for any. Empty for none. --expose / --no-expose , --path=<path> Whether to serve it over HTTP, and where (default /mcp/<name> ). A path another gateways/ entry uses is refused. The tool list is written out when you run the command, so a tool added later has to be added to mcp/<name>.bx . The served route has no authentication of its own: keep it off public networks or put it behind a proxy that checks a credential. Agent.yaml is edited by inserting lines only, so its comments and layout stay as they are. If the list cannot be extended that way (written on one line, say), or the definition is a class-based Agent.bx , nothing is changed and the error carries the entry to paste. A server the agent already uses, by name or address, is refused. add gateway Adds one way in to the agent: a chat platform, the web chat UI, or the HTTP API. (A hosted MCP route is added with add mcp server .) bxAgents add gateway telegram # polls Telegram, no public address needed bxAgents add gateway slack --env=botTokenEnvVar=ACME_BOT,appTokenEnvVar=ACME_APP --policy=steer bxAgents add gateway web --auth=key # the browser chat page, behind a random shared key bxAgents add gateway api --path=/api/chat bxAgents add gateway # asks which The platforms are the ones the new wizard offers: telegram , slack , discord , whatsapp-cloud , teams , twilio , github , email and signal . Flag Meaning --name=<name> The file, gateways/<name>.bx , or the second positional. Defaults to the type. A name in use is refused. --env=<config=NAME,...> Chat platforms: which variable holds which credential, for example botTokenEnvVar=ACME_BOT . Without it the usual names are used ( SLACK_BOT_TOKEN , ...). Only names go in the gateway file; an empty stub for each goes in .env . --policy=queue\|reject\|steer\|interrupt Chat platforms: what to do with a message that arrives while the agent is still answering. Written to Agent.yaml's gatewaySession unless it is the default queue . --path=<path> web and api : where it is served ( /chat and /api/chat by default). A path another gateway uses is refused. --auth=open\|key\|users web : anyone who can reach it, a random shared key kept in .env as CHAT_UI_API_KEY , or named users. --profiles=a,b web : the project's profiles people can pick in the chat (see Choosing the model ). Asked only when the project has profiles; none keeps the page on the agent's own model. --users=<name:hash,...> web with users : each hash comes from bxAgents hash-password . A password is never taken as a flag; at a terminal you type it, hidden, and only its hash is stored. After a chat platform is added, the output lists the steps that happen outside the project (creating the bot, a public address, a daemon) and which .env variables to fill in; bxAgents doctor reports any that are still not set. The HTTP API route has no authentication unless agentApi.tokenEnvVar is set in Agent.yaml . add subagent Adds a subagent: a whole agent under subagents/<name>/ with its own model, tools, MCP servers, memory and guard, wired into a parent's subAgents list. At a terminal it asks the same questions as new (purpose, model, tools, search, files, memory, MCP, guard); the questions only a whole project needs (shape, channels, deploy) are left out. bxAgents add subagent researcher # asks bxAgents add subagent writer --model=openai/gpt-5 --description="Writes the answer" bxAgents add subagent checker --model=claude --parent=writer --with=search --search=brave --guard=flag Flag Meaning --name=<name> The folder, or the first positional. A name any agent in the project already has is refused. --parent=<folder> The agent that delegates to it: . for the root (the default) or the folder of another subagent, which is how they nest. --model=<provider/model> Required without a terminal, unless --profile is given. --profile=<name> Use one of the project's profiles instead of a model, as the main agent can with profile: . At a terminal, a project that has profiles is asked which to use. --description , --with , --search , --files , --files-dir , --memory , --mcp , --guard The same as new . Writes subagents/<name>/Agent.yaml (with the environments.test mock model, so bxAgents test needs no key) and instructions.md , and adds an empty .env stub for each key the choices need. The name is inserted into the parent's subAgents without rewriting the file, so comments and order stay as they were. If the parent is a class, or its list is written in a shape that cannot be extended by inserting, nothing in it is changed and the line to add is printed. Packages a choice needs ( bx-playwright for browsing) are named for you to add to box.json . add skill Adds a custom skill of your own: skills/<name>/SKILL.md , in the Claude Agent Skills shape. It goes into source control with the project and into every build. bxAgents add skill release-notes --description="Use this skill when writing release notes" bxAgents add skill # asks Flag Meaning --name=<name> The folder, or the first positional. Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. A skill that already exists is refused. --description=<text> One sentence starting "Use this skill when". The model reads it to decide whether to load the skill, so it is the part that matters. Without it a TODO is written for you to replace. Skills are not wired to an agent: every skill in the build is available to the model. Skills from skills.boxlang.io are not added here; they are installed, not written. add provider Adds the settings every call to one provider starts from, under providers: in the root Agent.yaml (bx-ai's providers setting): the temperature, longest answer and timeout, whichever model or profile is used. bxAgents add provider openai --temperature=0.2 --timeout=60 bxAgents add provider # asks Flag Meaning --provider=<id> , or the first positional A provider bx-ai knows. One that already has settings is refused. --temperature , --max-tokens , --timeout At least one is needed. Written as params ( temperature , max_tokens ) and options ( timeout ). The provider's key is never asked for: its usual variable ( OPENAI_API_KEY ) gets an empty stub in .env . The entry is inserted without rewriting the file, so comments and order stay. Needs an Agent.yaml at the root. add profile Adds a named combination of provider, model, settings and key variable under profiles: in the root Agent.yaml (bx-ai's profiles setting).
