title: Lesson 2: What Is BxAgents?
body:
What Is BxAgents? Most agent frameworks wire tools, skills, routes and schedules together at request time , on every boot. BxAgents does the opposite: bxAgents build runs discovery, validation and code generation exactly once , producing a plain ColdBox application under .build/app/ . Starting it afterwards - via bxAgents serve , a real boxlang-miniserver process, or a portable .bxa deployed anywhere BoxLang runs - is then just booting an ordinary app. No convention scanning, no dynamic file walking, no build-time work deferred into the request path. flowchart LR A["your convention tree
Agent.yaml, tools/, skills/, ..."] -->|"bxAgents build"| B[".build/app/
a plain ColdBox application"] B -->|"bxAgents serve / chat / invoke"| C["running agent"] B -->|"bxAgents package"| D["dist/name-version.bxa"] D -->|"bxAgents deploy"| E["a real target"] style B fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 Folders are the API Agent.yaml and instructions.md are the only files that matter to get started. Every other convention folder - tools/ , skills/ , subagents/ , gateways/ , schedules/ , mcp/ , interceptors/ , modules/ - is optional and only shapes the generated output if it exists and has content in it . You add conventions as you actually need them, not up front. Agent.yaml defines the agent Agent.yaml is plain settings - a name, a model, and any optional extras - and the build turns it into a real BX AI agent. No code is needed for most agents. You'll write your first one in Lesson 5 . When the definition itself needs code (hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code), there is an advanced option: a class-based Agent.bx that extends BX AI's own AiAgent , which the build instantiates as-is. Lesson 5 ends with when to reach for it. What build actually produces Your convention tree on the left, the plain ColdBox application build turns it into on the right: your-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml ├── instructions.md ├── tools/ ├── skills/ ├── subagents/ ├── gateways/ ├── schedules/ ├── mcp/ ├── interceptors/ └── modules/ .build/app/ ├── Application.bx ├── config/ │ ├── ColdBox.bx │ ├── WireBox.bx │ ├── Router.bx │ └── Scheduler.bx ├── agent/ │ └── GeneratedAgentFactory.bx ├── tools/ skills/ mcp/ ├── handlers/ interceptors/ └── index.bxm Why this matters Rebuilding an unchanged project produces byte-identical output, down to a hash- stamped manifest recording exactly what went into the build (more on that in Lesson 20 ). That's the whole point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, rather than deferring any of it into request handling. See BxAgents home and The Build Pipeline for more detail whenever you want it. Next: Lesson 3 - Installing BxAgents

title: Lesson 3: Installing BxAgents
body: Installing BxAgents BxAgents is a BoxLang module. It needs two things on the machine that runs it: A BoxLang runtime. BxAgents itself, which bundles everything else it needs ( bx-ai , bx-sqlite , bx-ftp , bx-mail , bx-yaml , and ColdBox with its modules for the apps it generates). BoxLang 1.18.0 or later is required. 1 Install BoxLang Follow the official BoxLang installation guide . The quick installer also sets up ~/.boxlang/bin on your PATH , which is where module-provided executables (like BxAgents' own bxAgents command) land. 2 Install BxAgents install-bx-module bx-agents This fetches the module, with its bundled dependencies, into your BoxLang modules directory ( ~/.boxlang/modules by default, or boxlang_modules/ with --local ). 3 Verify it worked bxAgents --version bxAgents --help --help lists all 16 verbs ( new , add , build , test , serve , chat , invoke , package , deploy , inspect , clean , hash-password , token , notes , doctor , skills ) with a one-line summary of each. You'll use most of them in this course. The bxAgents command BxAgents declares a native executable in its box.json : "boxlang": { "moduleName": "bxagents", "executable": "bxAgents" } The installer turns that into a bxAgents wrapper script on your PATH . bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 is shorthand for the longer, always-equivalent form: boxlang module:bxagents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 This course uses the short bxAgents <verb> form throughout. Optional, for later lessons serve , chat --server and invoke --server ( Lesson 8 ) additionally need the standalone boxlang-miniserver binary on PATH . None of them is required to follow along with build , plain chat , test , package , inspect , clean or new . See Installation for the full reference page. Next: Lesson 4 - Scaffolding Your First Agent

title: Lesson 4: Scaffolding Your First Agent
body: Scaffolding Your First Agent With BoxLang and BxAgents installed ( Lesson 3 ), scaffold your first project: bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 --model is required - a provider/model slug (you'll see exactly how this gets parsed in Lesson 5 ). --name and --description are optional; --name defaults to the target directory's own name. new refuses to run if the target already contains an Agent.yaml or Agent.bx . What gets created my-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml ├── instructions.md ├── tools/ ├── skills/ ├── subagents/ ├── gateways/ ├── schedules/ ├── mcp/ ├── interceptors/ ├── modules/ └── tests/ ├── box.json └── specs/ └── AgentSpec.bx Plus a .env declaring BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime (matching serve 's own scoped runtime home) and a .gitignore ( .build/ , dist/ , .env ) - new never overwrites either if they already exist. BoxLang loads the .env from the project root itself, so this is also the place for your provider API keys. Every convention folder is created empty . You add files to the ones your agent actually needs and leave the rest alone - an empty tools/ folder has zero effect on the generated app. Agent.yaml looks like this (Pass --description and new adds a description: line.) # Your agent. Most agents need nothing more than this file and instructions.md. # For code in the definition (hooks, dynamic instructions), scaffold with --class. name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 environments: # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider. test: model: mock/mock-model That is the whole agent definition - more on each key in Lesson 5 . If you need code in the definition, pass --class and new scaffolds a class-based Agent.bx instead (also covered at the end of Lesson 5). The test suite runs itself new also runs box install in the scaffolded project root (its box.json lists TestBox), so bxAgents test ( Lesson 19 ) works immediately with no separate step. This is best-effort - if box isn't on PATH or the install fails, new still succeeds and just tells you to run it yourself. Pass --skipInstall to opt out entirely. Try it bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 cd my-agent ls You now have a real, if minimal, BxAgents project. The next four lessons walk through what's actually required to run it. Next: Lesson 5 - The Agent Definition: Agent.yaml

title: Lesson 5: The Agent Definition - Agent.yaml
body: The Agent Definition - Agent.yaml Agent.yaml is the only required file in a BxAgents project (beside the instructions it points at). It is plain settings - a name, a model, and any optional extras - and the build turns it into a real BX AI agent . No code needed. name: my-agent description: A helpful assistant model: openai/gpt-5 instructions: | You are a helpful assistant. That is a complete agent. bxAgents new scaffolds this shape for you (see Lesson 4 ), with the system prompt in an instructions.md beside it (see Lesson 6 ). Info A folder holds one agent definition. An Agent.yaml together with an Agent.bx (or an Agent.yml ) in the same folder is an error, and the build names both files so you can keep one. The keys Key What it does name The agent's name. Also its WireBox binding key, so it must be unique across the whole project. model A provider/model slug (see below). description Optional. instructions Inline system prompt. An instructions.md beside the file wins when both exist. tools Module tools this agent gets, as item@module or *@module (see Lesson 9 ). toolOptions Options for a module's tools, keyed by module name. subAgents Names of sibling folders under subagents/ (see Lesson 11 ). mcpServers Remote MCP servers the agent can call (see Lesson 17 ). security , memory , checkpointer Guardrails, conversation memory and human-in-the-loop state. gatewaySession How chat gateways queue sessions (see Lesson 14 ). agentApi The always-on agent route. environments Per-environment overrides (see below). An unknown key is an error that lists the valid ones, so a typo such as modle: can never quietly do nothing. Wrong types and empty values are errors too. Info The checkpointer is the one thing the build fills in unasked. An agent reachable from a gateway with no checkpointer has silently broken human-in-the-loop, so a definition that sets none still gets the cache default. The model slug model is BxAgents' own convention - bx-ai itself takes provider and model as two separate arguments. BxAgents splits the slug on the first / only : model value provider model openai/gpt-5 openai gpt-5 openrouter/anthropic/claude-x openrouter anthropic/claude-x mock/mock-model mock mock-model mock is a real provider that never makes a network call - useful for tests (see Lesson 19 ) and for following this course with no API key at all. Adding settings Other settings are just more keys: name: with-mcp-servers-agent model: openai/gpt-5 mcpServers: - https://example.com/mcp Environment overrides environments maps an environment name ( production , development , or any custom name) to a block of overrides: name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 environments: production: model: openai/gpt-5-mini test: model: mock/mock-model The active environment resolves, highest wins: --environment CLI flag > BX_AGENTS_ENV env var > "development" default. bxAgents build --environment=production picks it up. Only the active block is applied, on top of the top-level keys. You'll use this exact mechanism for the mock provider in your tests ( Lesson 19 ), which is why bxAgents new already gives you a test block. Full reference: Agent.yaml . When you need code: Agent.bx Agent.yaml covers almost every agent. Reach for the advanced class form, Agent.bx , only when the definition itself needs code: hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code, an overridden method, or computing the environment with detectEnvironment() . It is a real class extending bx-ai's AiAgent , which the build instantiates: class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "my-agent", description : "A helpful assistant", instructions: "You are a helpful assistant.", model : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } } Scaffold one with bxAgents new --class , or start in YAML and switch later: create the Agent.bx , move the settings across, and delete the Agent.yaml . Full reference: Agent.bx . Next: Lesson 6 - instructions.md and the System Prompt

title: Lesson 6: instructions.md and the System Prompt
body: instructions.md and the System Prompt instructions.md is optional - bxAgents new scaffolds a starter one for you to edit, but you have two equally valid choices for where your agent's system prompt lives: Set instructions inline in Agent.yaml . Drop an instructions.md file beside Agent.yaml and let the build wire it in. Letting the file win If instructions.md exists, the build emits: withInstructions( fileRead( "instructions.md" ) ) which wins over an inline instructions in Agent.yaml (or whatever a class set). This is the more common pattern in practice - it keeps the prompt as plain text you can edit without touching BoxLang code, and it's easy to diff in a pull request. # instructions.md You are a helpful assistant for a small hardware store. Be concise. If a customer asks about a product you don't have information on, say so rather than guessing. Setting it inline instead name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 instructions: | You are a helpful assistant. Keep answers short. Do this for a short prompt, or when you'd rather keep everything about the agent in one file. If both exist, instructions.md wins; if neither exists, the build fails and says so. A prompt that must be generated or templated in code belongs in the advanced class-based Agent.bx (see the end of Lesson 5 ). Which one should you pick? Start with instructions.md - it's what bxAgents new scaffolds, it's the simplest mental model ("the system prompt is this file"), and it plays nicely with the rest of this course, which assumes plain-text prompts throughout. Reach for the inline instructions key only for a short prompt, and for code only once you have a concrete reason to (templating, environment-specific prompts assembled from smaller pieces, etc.). Try it Open the instructions.md that Lesson 4 's bxAgents new created and write a real system prompt for whatever kind of agent you want to build in this course - a support bot, a code reviewer, anything. You'll build and run it in the next two lessons. Next: Lesson 7 - Building Your Agent

title: Lesson 7: Building Your Agent
body:
Building Your Agent With Agent.yaml and instructions.md in place, build your project: bxAgents build This runs the full build pipeline - config resolution, discovery, validation, code generation, manifest normalization - and writes a real ColdBox application to .build/app/ , plus .build/manifest.json . The five phases, in order flowchart TD A["1 · Resolve config"] --> B["2 · Discover"] B --> C{"3 · Validate"} C -->|"any error"| X["Build throws.
.build/app is never written"] C -->|"clean"| D["4 · Generate"] D --> E["5 · Normalize + write manifest"] E --> F[".build/manifest.json
+ .build/app"] style C fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 style X fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 style F fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 Resolve config - loads Agent.yaml (or a class-based Agent.bx , calling its configure() ) and the active environment override, then deep-merges any boxlang.json / boxlang-{env}.json . Discover - walks the project and enumerates every convention folder into raw entries. Pure discovery - no interpretation of file contents yet. Validate - collects every error (never fails fast) plus warnings: duplicate tool/skill/model/subagent names, circular references, bad model/provider config, and more. If any errors were collected, the build throws here - .build/app is never written or touched. Generate - only reached once validation is clean. Interceptors, gateways, MCP, the router, the web UI (if any), the core app skeleton, a verbatim copy of tools/ / skills/ , and the scheduler, in that order. Normalize + write the manifest - produces the canonical .build/manifest.json . If your project fails validation build fails with every collected error, not just the first one - a duplicate tool name and an unknown model provider in the same project both get reported in one run. Idempotency Rebuilding an unchanged project produces byte-identical output, down to the manifest's per-file content hashes. This is the entire point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, instead of deferring it into every request. Useful flag: --verbose bxAgents build --verbose Prints one line per build phase live as it runs - what got resolved/discovered/ validated, per-phase counts, which agents ended up registered in config/WireBox.bx and under which names, whether a scheduler was found, and a final timing line. Silent otherwise, so it costs nothing when you don't need it. Try it cd my-agent bxAgents build --verbose You should see a .build/app/ directory appear, and a manifest describing exactly what went into it. You'll talk to this built agent in the next lesson. Full reference: The Build Pipeline . Next: Lesson 8 - Talking to Your Agent

title: Lesson 8: Talking to Your Agent
body: Talking to Your Agent Once you've built your project ( Lesson 7 ), there are three ways to run it - all load the exact same GeneratedAgentFactory.bx and build the exact same agent tree, so they never diverge from each other. chat - an interactive REPL bxAgents chat # fast, in-process bxAgents chat --server [--port=<port>] # full app, own throwaway server bxAgents chat --connect=http://127.0.0.1:8080 # full app, server you already run Uses BoxLang's own MiniConsole for line reading. Requires a real interactive terminal (it shells out to stty for raw mode - it won't work piped or non-interactively). Type exit or quit to leave. The default mode loads the generated factory directly in this process - fastest, but without anything ColdBox brings (no scheduler, no interceptors, no gateway registry). When that matters, --server boots a real miniserver and drives the REPL over HTTP against your project's always-on agent route, and --connect does the same against a server you already have running. Both HTTP modes stream the reply token by token and carry the server's threadId across turns, so a session is one conversation rather than a series of unrelated first messages. invoke - one non-interactive turn bxAgents invoke --message="What's the weather in Boston?" [--json] Exists for scripting and CI, where chat 's TTY requirement is a hard blocker. By default this loads the generated factory in-process, the same path chat uses internally, just without the REPL loop - no serve prerequisite at all. --json prints {"response": "..."} instead of plain text. Add --server to instead launch a real, throwaway boxlang-miniserver process and send the message as a genuine HTTP request to your project's always-on agent route - no gateways/ entry needed (those come in Lesson 13 ). Like serve , it needs boxlang-miniserver on PATH . serve - a real HTTP server bxAgents serve --port=8080 Requires a prior build and requires boxlang-miniserver on PATH (see Lesson 3 ). Launches a real server process pointed at .build/app , scoped to its own .build/runtime BoxLang home so each project's compiled-class cache stays isolated. Warning The very first request to a freshly booted app's toAi() route can transiently fail - a genuine ColdBox/WireBox lazy-injection race, not a BxAgents bug. It succeeds reliably after that. Send a warm-up request before relying on a freshly deployed route under load. Testing without a real API key Every one of these needs a real model to talk to a real provider - but you don't need one yet. Add a test environment override to Agent.yaml (covered fully in Lesson 19 ): environments: test: model: mock/mock-model then bxAgents build --environment=test && bxAgents chat runs entirely against bx-ai's built-in mock provider - no network call, no API key. Try it export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... # or use the mock override above bxAgents chat Say hello to the agent you scaffolded and wrote instructions for in Lessons 4-6 . It's a real, running agent - you just haven't given it anything to do yet. That starts next lesson. Full reference: Quick Start , CLI Reference . Next: Lesson 9 - Giving Your Agent Tools
headings: Testing without a real API key

title: Lesson 9: Giving Your Agent Tools
body: Giving Your Agent Tools Any .bx file under tools/ (searched recursively, so tools/nested/Search.bx works too) that declares an @AITool -annotated function becomes a callable tool for your agent. // tools/Greeter.bx class { @AITool( "Say hello to someone by name." ) function sayHello( name ) { return "Hello, " & arguments.name & "!"; } } BxAgents doesn't scan or interpret @AITool annotations itself at build time - it just discovers one entry per .bx file (for name-collision checking) and copies the whole tools/ folder verbatim into the generated app. At startup, the generated app calls bx-ai's own scanner ( aiToolRegistry().scan( "tools" ) ), which does the real reflection work. This statement is only emitted at all if your project actually has a tools/ folder with files in it. Whose tools are they? An agent gets its own tools/ folder and nothing else: a root agent's tools are not given to its subagents, and the other way round. Tools that modules register with bx-ai (its built-ins, bx-playwright , ...) are only attached when the agent asks for them in Agent.yaml : tools: - now@bxai - "*@bxplaywright" See Agent.yaml for the details. Naming The discovered entry name is the file's own base name - Greeter.bx becomes Greeter . Two tool files with the same base name, even in different subfolders (since discovery is flat by base name), fail validation with a duplicate-name error. What's excluded Dotfiles are ignored by discovery, and .env /dotfiles inside tools/ are never copied into the build output even if present. Rebuilds are clean tools/ is copied with a wipe-then-write strategy on every build - a file you delete from your project's tools/ folder never lingers as stale output from a previous build. Try it Add a real tool to the agent you've been building: // tools/GetTime.bx class { @AITool( "Get the current server time." ) function now() { return dateTimeFormat( now(), "yyyy-mm-dd HH:nn:ss" ); } } Rebuild and chat with it: bxAgents build bxAgents chat > What time is it? Full reference: tools/ . Next: Lesson 10 - Packaging Skills

title: mcp/
body:
mcp/ MCP (Model Context Protocol) works two directions - consuming remote servers, and hosting your own. flowchart LR subgraph consume["CONSUMING - declared on Agent.yaml via mcpServers"] direction LR AG["your agent"] -->|"calls out at runtime"| RM["a remote MCP server
https://example.com/mcp"] end subgraph host["HOSTING - one file per server under mcp/"] direction LR TL["tools/
your @AITool functions"] -->|"a named SUBSET"| MS["mcpServer( 'localServer' )
registered at onApplicationStart()"] MS --> GW["a gateways/ entry with exposes: mcp
route( '/mcp/tools' ).toMCP()"] GW -->|"reachable over HTTP"| OC["some outside MCP client"] end style consume fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#004085 style host fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 Nothing links the two: an agent consuming remote servers need not host one, and a hosted server is reachable only if a gateways/ entry exposes it. Tip bxAgents add mcp client github adds a server to Agent.yaml with its credential as an environment placeholder, and bxAgents add mcp server writes the mcp/ file and the gateways/ entry that serves it. See add . Consuming remote servers Declared directly on Agent.yaml (not a file under mcp/ ), via mcpServers : # Agent.yaml name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 mcpServers: - https://example.com/mcp - url: https://other.com/mcp name: other Each entry is either a bare URL string or a mapping. A mapping can carry the credentials the server wants: mcpServers: - name: github url: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ token: ${env.GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN} - url: https://other.com/mcp headers: X-Api-Key: ${env.OTHER_API_KEY} timeout: 20000 Key Meaning url Required. The server's address name A label for the file. It is not sent to the server token A bearer token. Must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder: a token written in the file is a build error password , user Basic authentication. password must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder headers Extra request headers. Values can use ${env.NAME} timeout Milliseconds allowedHosts The host names the server's address may have, for example [api.example.com, "*.example.com"] . *.example.com matches any subdomain, not example.com itself. A request to any other host is refused before anything is sent redirects false treats a redirect answer as a failure and never follows it maxResponseBytes Refuses an answer longer than this many characters handshake true sends the MCP initialize handshake before the first call prefix Tools are named prefix__tool , so two servers cannot clash toolFilter A list of tool names; only these are given to the agent Placeholders are replaced with the environment variable when the app starts , never at build time, so a secret stays out of the project and out of a packaged .bxa . A variable that is not set fails the agent at startup and names it; one that is set but empty lets the agent start, the server refuses the connection, and bx-ai logs that and carries on without that server's tools. Any other key is a build error that lists the valid ones. The entries are passed into the generated aiAgent(mcpServers: [...]) call. No network connection is ever attempted at build time - reachability is a runtime concern; an unreachable server at build time is not a build error. This section is for servers reached over the web; servers that run as a program on the agent's machine are next. bxAgents new offers GitHub, Stripe, Notion, Atlassian, Cloudflare, Supabase and Git and writes the entry and the .env stub for you. Subagents can declare their own mcpServers independently - each node in the agent tree gets its own resolved list. Servers that run as a program An entry with command starts an MCP server as a program on the machine that runs the agent, and talks to it over the program's standard input and output: mcpServers: - name: git command: [uvx, mcp-server-git] prefix: git toolFilter: [git_status, git_diff, git_log] - name: browser command: [bxplaywright, mcp] env: PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY: ${env.PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY} cwd: . Key Meaning command Required. A list: the program, then its arguments. It is never run through a shell name A label for the file env Environment variables for the program. A variable whose name contains KEY , TOKEN , SECRET , PASSWORD or CREDENTIAL must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder cwd The folder the program starts in inheritEnv false starts it with only env . Default true maxRestarts How many times in a row a program that died is started again. Default 2 timeout Milliseconds per request prefix , toolFilter As for web servers The program starts on the first call and is closed when the app stops. command cannot be combined with url , and the keys that only make sense for a web server ( token , headers , user , password , allowedHosts , redirects , maxResponseBytes , handshake ) are a build error on it. When the app starts, the programs your agents declare become bx-ai's mcp.stdio.allowedCommands setting, so the process starts only what the project declared. A list you set yourself (for example in .boxlang.json ) is left alone and must name the programs. bxAgents doctor warns when a program is not on the PATH. A program runs with your user's rights on the machine that hosts the agent. Read what you start, and use toolFilter to limit what the agent may call. Hosting a local server Each mcp/*.bx file is a local MCP server your project hosts, exposing a subset of your tools/ as MCP tools: // mcp/localServer.bx class { function configure() { return { description : "Internal tools MCP server", version : "1.0.0", cors : "*", // optional - CORS origin(s) allowed to call this server; omit for none tools : [ "sayHello" ] // names of tools already declared under tools/ }; } } The entry's discovered name is its filename ( localServer.bx → localServer ), not any name field inside its own configure() struct - a project may still set one for documentation, but it's ignored for naming/registration purposes. cors is optional and defaults to an empty string (no CORS header) when omitted - passed straight through as mcpServer() 's 4th positional argument. At build time, the file is copied verbatim into the generated app's mcp/ folder, and a registration statement is emitted into Application.bx 's onApplicationStart() : mcpServer( "localServer", "Internal tools MCP server", "1.0.0", "*" ) .registerTool( aiToolRegistry().get( "sayHello" ) ) mcpServer(name, ...) is a global, name-keyed singleton getter in bx-ai - registering it once at startup is all that's needed; there's no WireBox mapping involved (unlike the agent-exposure singleton used by toAi() ). Exposing a local server over HTTP A local mcp/* server isn't reachable over HTTP on its own - pair it with a gateways/ exposure entry naming it as the target : // gateways/expose-mcp.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "localServer" }; } } Validation An mcpServers entry (struct form) needs a url or a command , not both and not neither. An mcpServers entry that's neither a non-empty string nor a struct fails validation. A command must be a list of non-empty words. A key for the other kind of server, an env secret written in the file, and a mistyped allowedHosts , redirects , handshake , prefix or toolFilter fail validation. A gateways/ entry with exposes: "mcp" and a target that doesn't match any discovered mcp/* entry fails validation.

Exposing a local server over HTTP

title: Models and profiles
body: Models and profiles Which model an agent uses is written in Agent.yaml . The build maps it onto bx-ai's settings, so you never write a boxlang.json for it. The names are bx-ai's own: provider , model , params , options , providers , profiles . provider: openai # the default model model: gpt-5 params: { temperature: 0.2 } providers: # settings for another provider claude: { params: { max_tokens: 4000 }, options: { timeout: 90 } } profiles: # named combinations fast: { description: Cheap and quick, provider: openai, model: gpt-5-mini, params: { temperature: 0 } } planner: { description: Careful planning, provider: claude, model: claude-opus-4, apiKeyEnv: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY } defaultProfile: fast # optional embeddings: { provider: openai, model: text-embedding-3-small } speech: { provider: openai, model: tts-1, voice: nova } transcription: { provider: openai, model: whisper-1 } image: { provider: openai, model: gpt-image-1, size: 1024x1024 } The default model provider , model and params are the model every agent uses when it says nothing else. model: openai/gpt-5 still works as shorthand for provider: openai plus model: gpt-5 . params are request parameters such as temperature and max_tokens . options (timeout and similar) apply to the default provider. Other providers providers holds params and options for a provider by name, for the ones you use through a profile or a subagent. bxAgents add provider writes one for you. The key for each provider is read from its usual environment variable ( OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , ...); bxAgents doctor tells you when one is missing. Profiles A profile is a named combination: a provider, a model, params, options and the name of the environment variable that holds its key. It can carry a description . Key Meaning description For people and the terminal and web pickers. provider , model What it runs on. A profile without a provider uses the default provider. params , options Layered on top of the provider's and the default's: params from the default, then the provider, then the profile. apiKeyEnv The name of the variable that holds the key. A key itself is never written in Agent.yaml ; a profile that has one is refused. A profile cannot be named default or like a provider ( openai , claude , ...), because both are selected by name. defaultProfile picks which profile is used when nothing asks for another one. bxAgents add profile writes a profile (and --default the defaultProfile ) without touching the rest of the file; see add profile . Which agent uses what An agent uses its own profile: , else its own model: (a provider/model slug), else the default. Every subagent inherits the root's settings, and may set its own model or profile : # subagents/planner/Agent.yaml name: planner profile: planner providers , profiles , defaultProfile , params and the capability keys apply to the whole app, so they belong in the project's own Agent.yaml ; a subagent that sets them fails validation. Capability defaults embeddings , speech , transcription and image set bx-ai's defaults for aiEmbed() , aiSpeak() , aiTranscribe() and aiImage() . They do not take profiles. bx-ai has one audio provider, so speech and transcription must name the same one. bxAgents add capability writes one; see add capability . Validation and tests bxAgents build checks all of the above by bx-ai's own rules and names the file and the key. Under bxAgents test every profile runs on the mock provider, so a test never reaches the network. How it reaches bx-ai The build writes the settings to config/bxai-settings.json in the app, and the app merges them into bx-ai's settings when it starts, before ColdBox boots and builds the agents. They travel with the app wherever it runs ( serve , a .bxa , a container).

title: modules/
body: modules/ modules/ holds BoxLang module dependencies your agent needs - one immediate subfolder per module, discovered by folder name (not recursive - only the top level of modules/ is enumerated). modules/ └── my-extra-module/ ├── module.json └── ... Declaring dependencies between modules A module folder may include a module.json with a dependsOn array naming other modules/* entries by folder name: { "dependsOn": [ "some-other-module" ] } This is BxAgents' own dependency-declaration convention for validation purposes - it is independent of BoxLang's own module-loading mechanism. Info Today build validates modules/ and records each entry (with a content hash) in the manifest , but it does not copy the folders into the generated app or load them. To give the generated app a library, use the project lib/ folder described in Installation . Validation A module.json that isn't valid JSON fails the build with a parse error naming the offending module. A dependsOn entry naming a module that isn't itself a discovered modules/* folder fails validation ("depends on unknown module"). Circular dependencies are rejected the same way subagent cycles are - full cycle path reported, DFS-based detection, no code generation happens until the graph is acyclic. A module.json is entirely optional - a module folder with none is assumed to have no declared dependencies.

title: Quick Start
body: Quick Start This walks through the full lifecycle of a BxAgents project: scaffold, edit, build, run. 1. Scaffold a project bxAgents new my-agent At a terminal this asks what the agent should do (its model, tools, MCP servers, channels, how people reach it, where it deploys) and writes the project to match; see the new wizard . To skip the questions, pass a model: bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 --model is a provider/model slug - see the model slug for how it's parsed. --name and --description are optional; --name defaults to the target directory's own name. This creates: my-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml ├── instructions.md ├── tools/ ├── skills/ ├── subagents/ ├── gateways/ ├── schedules/ ├── mcp/ ├── interceptors/ ├── modules/ └── tests/ ├── box.json └── specs/ └── AgentSpec.bx Plus a .env (with BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime ; put your provider API keys there too) and a .gitignore . BoxLang loads the .env from the project root itself. This is the minimal starter - the default when --template is omitted. new can also scaffold one of 7 other built-in starters ( --template=webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent ), each adding a bit of pre-wired content (a gateway, a scheduler) on top of the same skeleton, or skip scaffolding entirely and create the project from an existing GitHub repo ( --repo=owner/repo ) or a ForgeBox package ( --forgebox=<slug> ) instead - see the CLI Reference for the full list and how each one works. The agent is defined by an Agent.yaml by default; pass --class to scaffold the advanced, class-based Agent.bx instead (see Agent.bx ). Agent.yaml looks like this ( --description adds a description: line): # Your agent. Most agents need nothing more than this file and instructions.md. # For code in the definition (hooks, dynamic instructions), scaffold with --class. name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 environments: # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider. test: model: mock/mock-model The agent is just this file plus instructions.md . See Agent.yaml for every key. Every convention folder is created empty - add files to the ones your agent actually needs and delete (or just ignore) the rest. 2. Edit Open instructions.md and write the agent's system prompt, and adjust name , description or model in Agent.yaml as you like. Add a tool: // tools/Greeter.bx class { @AITool( "Say hello to someone by name." ) function sayHello( name ) { return "Hello, " & arguments.name & "!"; } } See the Conventions section for every other folder ( skills/ , subagents/ , gateways/ , schedules/ , mcp/ , interceptors/ , modules/ ). 3. Test it box install # once, to fetch testbox into lib/testbox (`new` already tried this for you) bxAgents test The scaffolded tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx passes out of the box - it builds your agent against the mock provider (no API key or network needed) and asserts on a scripted response. See tests/ for mockResponses() and the custom matchers ( toHaveCalledTool , etc.) available to your own specs. 4. Build bxAgents build Runs the full build pipeline - config resolution, discovery, validation, code generation, manifest normalization - and writes a real ColdBox application to .build/app/ , plus .build/manifest.json . Run bxAgents build --environment=production to build against an Agent.yaml environment override (see Agent.yaml ). If your project fails validation (duplicate tool names, an unknown model provider, a gateway entry with a bad path, ...) build fails with every collected error - not just the first one. 5. Run it Two ways to talk to the built agent - both load the exact same GeneratedAgentFactory.bx and build the exact same agent tree, so they never diverge: Interactively, from the terminal: bxAgents chat Over HTTP , via a real boxlang-miniserver process: bxAgents serve --port=8080 If your project has a gateways/* entry with { exposes: "agent", path: "/api/chat" } , the agent is now reachable at POST http://localhost:8080/api/chat/invoke (and /stream , /batch , /info - see gateways/ ). Warning The very first request to a freshly booted app's toAi() route can transiently fail. Send a warm-up request before relying on it under load. 6. Inspect, package, deploy bxAgents inspect # how the agent is composed: agents, tools, env vars, checks bxAgents package --version=1.0.0 # writes dist/my-agent-1.0.0.bxa + .sha256 bxAgents deploy --destination=/path/to/somewhere # copies the newest .bxa there See The Manifest and Deployment & Secrets . 7. Clean up bxAgents clean Removes .build/ and dist/ only - your source conventions ( Agent.yaml , tools/ , etc.) are never touched. Next steps Walk through every convention folder in Conventions . Look at the working sample projects in examples/ . See every verb's flags in CLI Reference .

title: schedules/
body: schedules/ schedules/Scheduler.bx - if present - is a real, hand-written ColdBox scheduler class , passed through into the build untouched (a plain file copy to config/Scheduler.bx , no generation, no translation): // schedules/Scheduler.bx class extends="coldbox.system.web.tasks.ColdBoxScheduler" { function configure() { task( "nightly" ) .call( () => getInstance( "SupportBot" ).run( "cleanup" ) ) .everyDayAt( "00:00" ) .withNoOverlaps() } } There's nothing BxAgents-specific about the body of that file - it's ColdBox's own scheduler DSL, in full: .every( 15, "minutes" ) , .everyDayAt( "09:00" ) , .onWeekdays( "08:30" ) , .everyWeekOn() , .startOn() / .endOn() / .between() , .when() , .withNoOverlaps() , before() / after() / onSuccess() / onFailure() hooks, timezones - anything ColdBox's ScheduledTask supports, this project doesn't limit or reinterpret. (An earlier version of this convention was a { cron, action } data shape translated into ColdBox's frequency-method DSL here - that translation only covered a narrow subset of cron and threw away everything else the real scheduler API offers, so it's gone. If you're migrating an old project, see below.) Tip bxAgents add schedule adds a task for you: say when it runs and what to tell the agent. See add . Retrieving an agent Every agent in the project's tree - the root project's own agent definition and every subagents/* entry, however deeply nested - is registered in the generated config/WireBox.bx under its own declared name (the name in its Agent.yaml , or, for a class-based Agent.bx , the one set via super.init() or a configure() -declared name overriding it). A schedule reaches whichever agent it wants with a plain getInstance( "TheAgentName" ) - no BxAgents-specific lookup, just WireBox, exactly like the getInstance() calls elsewhere in a ColdBox app. # subagents/researcher/Agent.yaml name: ResearchBot description: Researches a topic model: openai/gpt-5 // schedules/Scheduler.bx task( "weekly-digest" ) .call( () => getInstance( "ResearchBot" ).run( "summarize this week's findings" ) ) .everyWeekOn( 1, "08:00" ) Because name is now also a WireBox binding key, it must be unique across the whole project - build fails validation if two agents (root or subagent, at any depth) share a name, including two that both leave it unset and silently default to "BxAi" . See subagents/ for the distinction between a subagent's folder name (used to wire subAgents: [...] ) and its own declared name (used here). Validation build only ever looks for exactly one file: schedules/Scheduler.bx . Anything else in schedules/ (including old { cron, action } files from before this convention changed) is ignored - build emits a warning if schedules/ exists but has no Scheduler.bx , so a schedule that quietly stopped running is at least visible. Beyond that, schedules/Scheduler.bx is real code - the same kind of "we can't meaningfully validate this without a real ColdBox boot" territory as any other BoxLang class. A syntax error or a bad getInstance() name surfaces when the generated app actually boots ( serve ), not at build validation time. Migrating from the old { cron, action } convention Before, each file under schedules/ was its own { cron: "0 0 * * *", action: "cleanup" } entry, translated into a ColdBox frequency-method call against the single root "GeneratedAgent" binding. To migrate: delete those files, add one schedules/Scheduler.bx extending coldbox.system.web.tasks.ColdBoxScheduler , and for each old entry add a task( name ).call( () => getInstance( "TheAgentName" ).run( "action text" ) ) with whichever real ColdBox frequency method or .cron() call matches the old cron expression.
headings: Migrating from the old { cron, action } convention

title: skills/
body: skills/ Each immediate subfolder of skills/ that contains a SKILL.md file is one skill, following the Claude Agent Skills convention: YAML frontmatter ( name , description ) followed by a body of freeform instructions. skills/ └── greeting/ └── SKILL.md --- name: greeting description: How to greet people warmly. --- Always greet the user warmly and use their name if known. Tip bxAgents add skill <name> creates skills/<name>/SKILL.md with the frontmatter and a body to fill in. See add . Naming The skill's name is its frontmatter name: if present; otherwise it falls back to the folder name ( greeting/ with no frontmatter name would be discovered as greeting anyway, but an explicit name: always wins even if it differs from the folder). Two skills resolving to the same name fail validation with a duplicate-name error. A folder without a SKILL.md inside it is not discovered as a skill at all - it's simply ignored (useful for scratch subfolders, assets kept alongside a skill under a different structure, etc., as long as they don't sit directly under skills/ themselves without a SKILL.md ). Skills from the registry Skills from skills.boxlang.io are installed with bxAgents skills install <owner/repo/skill> , not copied by hand. They go in .agents/skills/ (bx-ai's own default folder), out of source control; .agents/skills.lock.json is committed and build restores from it. Both folders go into the build, and a skill in skills/ with the same name wins. See skills . How it's wired at runtime skills/ is copied verbatim into the generated app (same wipe-then-write, dotfile-excluding copy as tools/ ). The generated config/ColdBox.bx always points bx-ai's own skillsDirectory module setting at /skills : moduleSettings = { bxai : { skillsDirectory : "/skills" } } Info bx-ai's own default skillsDirectory is /.agents/skills - a different path than BxAgents' skills/ convention. The generator always overrides it explicitly so the app's skills/ folder is the one bx-ai actually loads from. Skills installed under your project's .agents/skills/ are copied into it at build time; you never need to set this yourself.

title: subagents/
body:
subagents/ subagents/ holds nested agents, each an ordinary BxAgents project of its own - an Agent.yaml + instructions.md (and optionally its own tools/ , skills/ , etc.). A subagent's tools/ belong to it alone, and its tools: list is its own; neither is inherited from or shared with its parent: my-agent/ ├── Agent.yaml # subAgents: [ researcher ] ├── instructions.md └── subagents/ └── researcher/ ├── Agent.yaml └── instructions.md A subagent is wired to its parent by name, declared in the parent's Agent.yaml subAgents list - the subagents/ FOLDER name to wire at build time: # Agent.yaml name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 subAgents: - researcher The same list in a class-based Agent.bx (the advanced form ) goes in configure() , distinct from super.init() 's own subAgents argument (which takes already-built AiAgent instances, not names). A project can mix the two forms: a YAML root with a class subagent, or the reverse. At build time, bx-ai's addSubAgent() wraps each built subagent instance as a callable tool on the parent automatically - there's no separate tool-wrapping step to write yourself. Tip bxAgents add subagent creates the folder, asks the same questions as new for its model and tools, and adds it to the parent's subAgents . --parent= nests it under another subagent. See add . Flat namespace, sibling references Every subagent - no matter how deeply another subagent's own config references it - lives directly under the root project's subagents/ folder. A subagent's own declared subAgents names reference sibling entries in that same root-level folder, not a folder nested under itself. This keeps the discovery/validation model simple: one flat directed graph over subagents/ 's immediate subfolders, rather than a tree that could nest arbitrarily deep on disk. Flat on disk, a graph in config, built bottom-up - the three views of the same project: flowchart LR subgraph disk["ON DISK - always flat, one level under the ROOT project"] direction TB R1["subagents/A/"] R2["subagents/B/"] R3["subagents/C/"] end subgraph declared["DECLARED - each definition's own subAgents list"] direction TB GA["A"] --> GB["B"] --> GC["C"] end subgraph built["BUILT - leaf-first, in GeneratedAgentFactory.bx"] direction TB O1["1. build C"] --> O2["2. build B
with the built C"] --> O3["3. build A
with the built B"] end disk -.->|"names resolve
against siblings"| declared declared -.->|"a parent needs its
children already built"| built style disk fill:#eef2f7,stroke:#5a6570 style declared fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#004085 style built fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 A cycle in the declared graph ( A -> B -> A ) is rejected at validation, before any of this is generated; a diamond (two parents sharing one descendant) is fine. Build order Subagents are built leaf-first (bottom-up): if A declares subAgents: ["B"] and B declares subAgents: ["C"] , the generated GeneratedAgentFactory.bx builds C , then B (passing in the built C instance), then A (passing in the built B instance) - never the other way around, since a parent's aiAgent() call needs its children's already-built instances. Validation A subagent name in subAgents that doesn't correspond to a real subagents/{name}/ folder (holding an Agent.yaml or Agent.bx ) fails validation with a clear "references unknown subagent [...]" error - this applies to every node's subAgents list, including the root project's own definition, not just nested subagents. Circular references ( A → B → A ) are rejected at validation time, with the full cycle path reported (e.g. A -> B -> A ), before any code generation happens. A "diamond" shape - two subagents both depending on the same shared descendant - is not a cycle and builds fine; only genuine cycles are rejected. A missing Agent.yaml / Agent.bx inside a discovered subagents/* folder is reported as its own validation error, and so is a folder holding both ( BxAgents.AmbiguousAgentDefinition ) - a folder holds one definition. Every node's own DECLARED name (root + every subagent's own definition) must be unique across the whole project - see below. Retrieving an agent from schedules/Scheduler.bx Two different names are in play, and they're not interchangeable: The folder name under subagents/ ( researcher above) is what subAgents: [ "..." ] references - it's purely a build-time wiring concern. The subagent's own declared name (its agent definition's name field, e.g. "ResearchBot" ) is what you retrieve it by at runtime - every agent in the tree (root + every subagent) is registered in config/WireBox.bx under this name, so schedules/Scheduler.bx (or any other WireBox-aware code) reaches it with a plain getInstance( "ResearchBot" ) . These two names can differ, and often will - the folder name is an implementation detail, the declared name is the one that matters everywhere else (prompts, WireBox retrieval). Because it's now also a WireBox binding key, build fails validation if two agents in the tree - however deeply nested - end up with the same declared name , including two that both leave it unset and silently share the "BxAi" default.

title: tests/
body: tests/ Every project scaffolded via bxAgents new gets a root box.json (declaring testbox as a development dependency, installed into lib/testbox ) and a ready-to-run tests/ folder with tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx , an example spec that passes out of the box. cd my-agent box install # fetches testbox into lib/testbox (new already ran this for you) bxAgents test Info Inspired by the coldbox-templates/boxlang template's own dedicated tests/ + box.json folder - adapted to BxAgents' own simpler testing story. Testing an agent is about its behavior (what it says, which tools it calls), not HTTP routing, so there's no Application.bx /ColdBox virtual app involved here at all. Writing a spec Extend bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec (a testbox.system.BaseSpec subclass) instead of testbox.system.BaseSpec directly: // tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx class extends="bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec" { function run() { describe( "my-agent", function() { it( "responds to a greeting", function() { mockResponses( [ "Hello! How can I help you today?" ] ) var response = agent.run( "Hi there" ) expect( response ).toContainText( "Hello" ) } ) } ) } } BaseAgentSpec builds your agent once per spec bundle ( beforeAll() ), against a throwaway temp copy of your project - it never touches your real .build/app , so running tests never clobbers (or is clobbered by) a real build / serve / package cycle. The built agent is exposed as agent . Testing against the mock provider By default, bxAgents test builds your agent using the test environment override in Agent.yaml (scaffolded automatically): # Agent.yaml environments: test: model: mock/mock-model A class-based Agent.bx expresses the same override as a test() method returning { model : "mock/mock-model" } . This means your tests need no API key and no network access out of the box - the same mock provider convention used throughout BxAgents' own test suite. Edit this override if you want a spec to run against a real provider instead (you'll need a real API key available in the environment running the tests). mockResponses( responses ) Scripts the agent's next replies, consumed in order - one per LLM round-trip, including the intermediate turns of a tool-calling loop: mockResponses( [ { toolCalls: [ { name: "getWeather", arguments: { city: "Miami" } } ] }, "It's sunny in Miami!" ] ) var response = agent.run( "What's the weather in Miami?" ) A plain string scripts a final reply. A { toolCalls: [ { name, arguments } ] } struct scripts a tool-call turn - the named tool actually executes for real (against your real tools/ implementation), and its real return value is what the next round-trip sees; only the LLM's own reply is scripted, never the tool's behavior. Custom matchers BaseAgentSpec registers a few matchers, tailored to testing agent behavior, via TestBox's own addMatchers() extension point - use them exactly like any built-in TestBox matcher, including negation ( notTo... ): Matcher Checks toContainText( "substring" ) The actual value (usually a response string) contains the given text, case-insensitively. toHaveCalledTool( "toolName" ) The agent's own recorded provider requests show it actually decided to invoke the named tool - not just that the tool exists. toHaveReceivedMessage( "substring" ) Some message actually sent to the provider (any role, any round-trip) contained the given text - useful for asserting your system prompt/instructions actually reached the model. expect( agent ).toHaveCalledTool( "getWeather" ) expect( agent ).notToHaveCalledTool( "getStockPrice" ) Running tests bxAgents test Runs your project's tests/specs/** via TestBox, in a fresh child process (so it never fights over BoxLang's own class-mapping caches with anything else you're running). Prints bundle/suite/spec counts and pass/fail/error/skipped totals, plus one line per failure, and exits non-zero if anything failed - suitable as a CI gate before deploy . Warning bxAgents test requires TestBox actually installed in lib/testbox ( box install in the project root; tests/testbox is also found, for projects scaffolded before box.json moved to the root) - it errors clearly, rather than silently reporting zero specs, if that hasn't been done yet.

title: The Build Pipeline
body:
The Build Pipeline bxAgents build runs a fixed sequence of phases, once, producing a plain ColdBox application. Nothing here runs again at request time - that's the whole point of build-time assembly. This page walks the phases in the exact order BuildPipeline.bx runs them. flowchart TD A["1 · Resolve config
AgentConfigResolver"] --> B["2 · Discover
ProjectDiscoverer"] B --> C{"3 · Validate
ProjectValidator"} C -->|"any error"| X["Build throws.
.build/app is never written or touched"] C -->|"clean
warnings never block"| D["4 · Generate"] D --> D1["1 Interceptors"] --> D2["2 Gateways"] --> D3["3 MCP"] --> D4["4 Router"] D4 --> D5["5 Web UI"] --> D6["6 Core app skeleton"] --> D7["7 Tools/skills copy"] --> D8["8 Runtime libraries"] --> D9["9 Scheduler"] D9 --> E["5 · Normalize + write
ManifestNormalizer"] E --> F[".build/manifest.json
+ .build/app - a plain ColdBox application"] style C fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 style X fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 style F fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 Validation is the gate: it collects every error rather than failing fast, and nothing is generated until it comes back clean. (Packaging into a .bxa is a deliberately separate step - see Deployment & Secrets - so a fast build → inspect → build again loop never pays a packaging cost it doesn't need.) 1. Resolve config AgentConfigResolver loads the agent definition ( Agent.yaml , or the class-based Agent.bx ), applies the active environment's overrides (the environments: block of an Agent.yaml , or the override method and configure() of an Agent.bx ), then deep-merges in boxlang.json / boxlang-{env}.json / miniserver.json / miniserver-{env}.json if present. Produces the single resolved config struct every later phase reads from. 2. Discover ProjectDiscoverer walks the project root and enumerates every convention folder ( tools/ , skills/ , subagents/ , gateways/ , mcp/ , interceptors/ , modules/ ) into raw { name, path, type } entries. schedules/ is the one exception - it's not a list of entries, just a single hasScheduler / schedulerPath pair, since it holds one real ColdBox scheduler file rather than a set of BxAgents-defined config entries. Pure discovery - no interpretation of file contents happens yet. 3. Validate ProjectValidator runs every validator and collects every error (never fail-fast) plus any warnings: duplicate tool/skill/model/subagent names, duplicate agent name s across the whole subagent tree (see subagents/ ), circular subagent/module references, the two gateway entry shapes, remote MCP config completeness, and model/provider validity. If any errors were collected, the build throws immediately here - no .build/app is written or touched. Warnings (e.g. a schedules/ folder with no Scheduler.bx in it) never block the build. 4. Generate Only reached once validation is clean. In order: Interceptors - InterceptorSplitter copies agent -scope interceptors into .build/app/interceptors , runtime -scope ones into a separate .build/runtime-interceptors directory, outside the app (BxAgents does not register those for you). Gateways - GatewayGenerator emits aiGatewayRegistry().register(...) statements for channel-adapter entries, and writes a small .build/app/handlers/*.bx webhook handler for each whatsapp-cloud , teams , twilio or github entry. If any entry is a push-style gateway (e.g. type: "telegram" ), it also produces the start-up statement that builds a single bx-ai GatewaySession (bundling every push-style gateway) bound to the project's root agent. MCP - McpGenerator copies local mcp/* servers into .build/app/mcp and emits their mcpServer(...).registerTool(...) registration statements. Router - RouterGenerator writes .build/app/config/Router.bx : the reserved /__bxagents agent route (unless agentApi.enabled is false ), one route(path).toAi(...) / toMCP(...) per exposure entry, a single route("/gateways").toAiGateway() if the project has any channel-adapter gateway, and one webhook route per whatsapp-cloud (GET+POST), teams , twilio or github push-style gateway present. Web UI - WebUiGenerator runs for any exposes: "webui" entry, writing the static /index.html , handlers/ChatUi.bx (the twenty-action API), models/ChatDb.bx (the SQLite store and its forward-only migrations, built at boot by a start-up statement rather than on whichever request touches the database first), the user models ( User , UserService , PasswordHasher ), and - only when apiKeyEnvVar is set - interceptors/WebUiAuthGate.bx . When users are declared it also writes the account seeder, interceptors/WebUiLoginGate.bx and handlers/ChatAuth.bx . It returns the resolved database config, which the next step needs. Core app skeleton - ColdBoxAppGenerator writes Application.bx , config/ColdBox.bx , config/WireBox.bx , agent/GeneratedAgentFactory.bx , and index.bxm , threading in every statement gathered above (gateway registrations, the GatewaySession start, MCP registrations, the web UI's store warm-up and account seeding, and - if tools/ has any files - a bare aiToolRegistry().scan("tools") call) into Application.bx 's onApplicationStart() . Interceptors are registered there too, one getInterceptorService().register(...) per agent-scope interceptor and web UI gate: a declarative interceptors array in config/ColdBox.bx never reaches ColdBox's interceptor service, so the generated config declares none. Every generated agent also now always receives a checkpointer ( withCheckpointer(...) , defaulting to a cache -backed aiMemory() if the project declares no checkpointer config and the class set none of its own) - without one, human-in-the-loop approval flows through any gateway other than cli fail outright. config/WireBox.bx maps every agent in the tree (root + every subagent) under its own declared name , not just the fixed root "GeneratedAgent" alias - see schedules/ . Each agent node's instructions.md is copied into the app as part of this step, mirroring the source layout under agent/ - the root project's to .build/app/agent/instructions.md , each subagent's to .build/app/agent/subagents//instructions.md - so every node keeps its own and the built app carries the file it reads at runtime. The factory reads all three of its runtime paths ( instructions.md , its own tools/ , and any class-based agent's copied Agent.bx ) through a small generated resolveAppPath() helper that resolves them relative to the factory's own location on disk, falling back to the build-time absolute path if that self-location doesn't resolve - which is what makes a packaged .bxa genuinely relocatable rather than runnable only on the machine that built it. For a project with a webui exposure it also turns session management on, registers the SQLite datasource (naming it as the app default via this.datasource ), creates the database's parent directory in onApplicationStart() - SQLite creates the file but never the folder holding it - and pins qb's grammar in config/ColdBox.bx . Tools/skills copy - ToolsSkillsCopier wipes and rewrites .build/app/tools and .build/app/skills verbatim from your project's own folders. Runtime libraries - RuntimeLibsCopier copies the ColdBox runtime bundled inside BxAgents into .build/app : coldbox/ plus modules/qb , modules/cbsecurity , modules/cbauth , modules/cbmailservices and their dependencies. A lib/ folder in your project (same layout) is copied afterwards and wins, which is how you add or override a library. The bundled copy exists only in an installed or built module, so a source checkout skips this step with a warning. Scheduler - SchedulerGenerator copies schedules/Scheduler.bx through to .build/app/config/Scheduler.bx untouched, if present - no generation, it's real ColdBox code you wrote yourself. 5. Normalize + write the manifest ManifestNormalizer produces the canonical, hash-stamped internal manifest from the discovery + resolved-config data, and the pipeline writes it to .build/manifest.json . Idempotency Rebuilding an unchanged project produces byte-identical output, down to the manifest's per-file content hashes - the entire point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, rather than deferring any of this work into request handling.

title: The Manifest
body: The Manifest Every build writes .build/manifest.json - BxAgents' own record of exactly what went into the generated app. bxAgents inspect reports whether a project was built and the manifest's version and file count in its build section (the manifest itself is a plain file you can open); bxAgents package copies a redacted version of it alongside the .bxa (see Deployment & Secrets ). Schema { "manifestVersion": "1.0.0", "generator": { "name": "bx-agents", "version": "dev" }, "agent": { "name": "my-agent", "description": "", "model": "openai/gpt-5", "environment": "development" }, "files": [ { "category": "tools", "name": "Greeter", "path": "tools/Greeter.bx", "hash": "..." } ] } Field Meaning manifestVersion Semver stamp for the manifest schema itself (currently 1.0.0 ) - package refuses to run if this is unset or malformed. generator.name / generator.version Always "bx-agents" / the version string stamped into the build: dev unless bxAgents build --generatorVersion=... says otherwise. agent Only safe, structural fields ( name , description , model , environment ) - never secrets. Secrets are never read into the manifest at all; they're resolved by bx-ai itself, live, at runtime. files One entry per discovered convention-folder item, sorted by category then path for deterministic ordering - independent of filesystem listing order. Content hashes Each files[] entry's hash is a SHA-256 of its content: A file : the hash of its content, with line endings normalized first (CRLF and LF checkouts of the same content hash identically). A directory (a skill folder, a subagent folder, a module folder): the hash of every contained file's own relativePath:contentHash , recursively, sorted for determinism - so renaming or editing any single file inside changes the whole folder's hash. This is what makes rebuilding an unchanged project produce an identical manifest: same categories, same ordering, same hashes, every time - and it's exactly why changing one tool file's content only ever changes that one entry's hash, nothing else. Compatibility policy manifestVersion exists so a future breaking change to this schema can be detected by anything reading manifest.json (a deploy target, a future inspect version, external tooling) - a tool encountering an unrecognized major version should refuse to guess at the shape and fail clearly, rather than silently misreading fields.

title: The new wizard
body: The new wizard Run bxAgents new in a terminal with no --model and it asks what the agent should do, then writes the project to match. Nothing in it is magic: every answer ends up in a file you can read, and the last screen prints the one-line command that would build the same project without any questions. bxAgents new my-agent It is a full-screen UI in the teal of the BxAgents logo. Arrow keys (or j / k ) move, Space ticks, Enter confirms, Esc goes back one question , Ctrl+C cancels and creates nothing. Answers you have given collapse to one line each above the current question. What it asks Stage What you choose What it writes Name, purpose The agent's name and a one-line description name , description in Agent.yaml Shape A single agent, a team, a scheduled agent, an MCP server The matching template Model A provider, then optionally a model name (Enter takes the provider's default) model , and a stub for the provider's <PROVIDER>_API_KEY in .env Model settings Whether to tune the model, then the temperature (0 to 2), the longest answer in tokens and the timeout in seconds. Enter leaves one unset params ( temperature , max_tokens ) and options ( timeout ) in Agent.yaml Tools Date and time, fetch pages, search the web, browse websites, files, images and speech A tools: list; browsing also adds bx-playwright to your box.json Search provider The built-in one, Brave, Tavily, Exa or Google A key stub in .env , and a line in instructions.md telling the agent which provider to use File tools Read only, all 19, or tool by tool, then the folders they may use toolOptions.bxai.allowedPaths Memory In memory, or saved to disk memory and checkpointer MCP servers GitHub, Stripe, Notion, Atlassian, Cloudflare, Supabase, Git mcpServers entries and token stubs Channels Web chat, HTTP API, Telegram, Slack, Discord, WhatsApp, Teams, SMS, GitHub, Email, Signal A gateways/*.bx file and the stubs it needs Web access Open, a shared key, or named users with passwords apiKeyEnvVar or users on the web chat entry Guard Flag, block or ignore suspicious input A security block Deploy Docker, DigitalOcean, SSH, SFTP, FTP, a local folder, or later deploy/<target>.json A stage whose answer you already gave as a flag is skipped and shown as answered. A stage that does not apply (the search provider when search is off) is skipped without a word. File tools never get the whole disk bx-ai ships 19 file tools but registers none of them. The wizard offers them, and always asks which folders they may use: the temp folder ( tmp ), the folder you run the agent from ( cwd ), or a path you type. It will not continue with none. There is no way to ask for unrestricted access from the wizard or from the flags; an empty list is refused because bx-ai reads an empty list as "everywhere". tools: - readFile@bxai - listDirectory@bxai toolOptions: bxai: allowedPaths: - tmp - cwd Secrets The wizard never asks you to type a secret that it stores. API keys and tokens go in .env as empty stubs, each under a comment saying where to get it. The files that use them hold only the variable's name . A web access key is generated for you (a random 64-character value) and written to .env , because it protects something you are about to run. A web chat password is hashed with the same PBKDF2 hasher as bxAgents hash-password ; only the hash reaches gateways/webui.bx , and it is safe to commit. .env is in the .gitignore the project is created with. MCP servers All servers in the picker are remote (HTTP) servers that the bundled bx-ai can connect to, listed with how risky they are. Each starts with its credential read from the environment when the app starts: mcpServers: - name: github url: "https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/" token: "${env.GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN}" Server Credential Risk GitHub GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN High: can open and merge pull requests, push files, trigger Actions Stripe STRIPE_AGENT_API_KEY High: moves money. Use a sandbox account first Notion NOTION_MCP_TOKEN Medium: edits and deletes pages. Tokens need a Business or Enterprise plan Atlassian ATLASSIAN_API_TOKEN Medium. Unverified: the header an API token goes in is not documented Cloudflare CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN High: DNS, Workers, billable resources, depending on the token Supabase SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN High: runs SQL. The address starts read-only Picking a high-risk server shows what it can do before you continue. Git runs as a program on your machine ( uvx mcp-server-git ), so it needs uv installed where the agent runs, and it works in the folder you start the agent from. The wizard writes it as a command entry; see programs as MCP servers . After it is created new runs box install (skip it with --skipInstall ), then prints what is left: the keys to fill in, how to chat, test, serve and deploy, and, for each channel you chose, the setup that happens outside the project. For WhatsApp that means the Meta app, the verify token and a public address; for Slack, Socket Mode and two tokens; for Signal, a running signal-cli . The same steps live on each gateway page . Without the wizard The wizard writes nothing a flag cannot. The last screen prints the command; this one came from a real run: bxAgents new support-bot --name=support-bot --model=claude --with=time,fetch,search --search=brave \ --mcp=github --channels=web,telegram --web-auth=key --guard=flag --deploy=docker --registry=ghcr:me/support-bot Flag Takes --with time , fetch , search , browse , files , media (a list) --search http , brave , tavily , exa , google --files , --files-dir read , all or a list of tool names; folders as tmp , cwd or absolute paths. Both are needed together --temperature A number from 0 to 2 --max-tokens , --timeout A positive whole number (tokens, seconds) --memory cache or file --mcp MCP server ids (a list) --channels web , api , or channel ids (a list) --web-auth open or key . Users need passwords, so they come from the wizard or from gateways/webui.bx --guard off , flag or block --deploy docker , digitalocean , ssh , sftp , ftp , local , with --registry=ghcr:owner/name (or dockerhub: , docr: ), --app , --region , --host , --user , --remote-path , --destination as the target needs A flag with a bad value stops the command and says what the flag accepts. The wizard turns on when: You run Result bxAgents new at a terminal The full-screen wizard bxAgents new in a pipe, or with --no-tui The same questions as numbered lines. Type back to go back bxAgents new --model=... No questions: a model means a script is calling. Add --wizard to be asked the rest bxAgents new --no-wizard or --yes No questions, flags and defaults only Set NO_COLOR for plain output. The Agent.yaml options the wizard writes need the default Agent.yaml , so they cannot be combined with --class .
